# jasy - full documentation

> Declarative PDFs and conformant XRechnung / ZUGFeRD / Factur-X e-invoices in pure TypeScript, in Node
> or the browser, as functions, Vue components or React components. Every page of https://jasy.dev/docs
> below, in order. The short index is https://jasy.dev/llms.txt.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs
Summary: jasy is a pure-TypeScript toolkit for generating PDFs and ZUGFeRD / XRechnung e-invoices.

# jasy

The name is short for **ja**vaScript ea**sy** PDF, and that is the whole goal: a pure-TypeScript
toolkit for building PDFs, and the first Node library that handles ZUGFeRD and XRechnung e-invoices
end to end - generate, validate and read. No Java, no headless browser, no upload. Your data never
leaves your machine.

## The packages

| Package           | What it does                                                            |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@jasy/pdf`       | the declarative, Flutter-style PDF engine                               |
| `@jasy/vue`       | author PDFs as Vue components, rendered in the browser or on a server   |
| `@jasy/react`     | author PDFs as React components, rendered in the browser or on a server |
| `@jasy/nuxt`      | the Nuxt module: zero-config PDFs on the client or a server route       |
| `@jasy/e-invoice` | ZUGFeRD / XRechnung: your data to a conformant PDF/A-3 and EN-16931 XML |
| `@jasy/cli`       | the `jasy` terminal: read, validate and export invoices                 |

## Install

Pick the package for what you want to do. jasy is in beta, and `latest` is the beta.

```bash
pnpm add @jasy/pdf             # build PDFs
pnpm add @jasy/vue vue          # author PDFs as Vue components
pnpm add @jasy/react @jasy/pdf react  # author PDFs as React components
npx nuxi module add @jasy/nuxt  # the Nuxt module
pnpm add @jasy/e-invoice        # build e-invoices (pulls @jasy/pdf in for you)
pnpm add -g @jasy/cli           # the command-line tool
```

## Where to next

- [**Creating PDFs**](/docs/pdf) - the engine, from a one-line hello to full layouts.
- [**PDFs in Vue**](/docs/vue) - author documents as Vue components, rendered in the browser.
- [**PDFs in Nuxt**](/docs/nuxt) - the zero-config module, client or server.
- [**PDFs in React**](/docs/react) - author documents as React components, rendered in the browser.
- [**E-invoices**](/docs/invoicing) - generate and validate ZUGFeRD / XRechnung.
- [**The CLI**](/docs/cli) - read, validate and export any invoice from your terminal.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf
Summary: Build your first PDF with @jasy/pdf in a few lines of TypeScript - in Node or the browser - then grow it into a full, paginated layout. No headless browser.

# Creating PDFs

`@jasy/pdf` lets you describe a document as a tree of components, the way you would build a user
interface, and writes the PDF byte stream itself. No headless browser, no Java. You compose a few
primitives - `Page`, `Column`, `Row`, `Box`, `Text` - and the engine lays them out.

## Install

```bash
pnpm add @jasy/pdf
```

To run a TypeScript file directly and get full type support, add [`tsx`](https://tsx.is) and the Node
type definitions as dev dependencies:

```bash
pnpm add -D tsx @types/node
```

## Your first PDF

Create a file, paste this in, and you have a one-page PDF. It works in any project, whether your
`package.json` uses `commonjs` or `module`.

```ts
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { Document, Page, Text, renderToBytes } from "@jasy/pdf";

async function build() {
  const doc = Document([
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56 }, [
      Text("Hello from jasy", { size: 28, bold: true, color: "#1450aa" }),
      Text("Declarative PDFs in pure TypeScript.", { size: 13, color: "gray" }),
    ]),
  ]);

  writeFileSync("hello.pdf", await renderToBytes(doc));
}

build();
```

Run it with [`tsx`](https://tsx.is) (or your own build step):

```bash
npx tsx hello.ts
```

Open `hello.pdf` and there it is. The shape never changes: a `Document` holds `Page`s, a `Page` holds
your content, and `renderToBytes` gives you a `Uint8Array` you can write to a file or stream to a
browser. Prefer a string? Use `renderPdf` instead.

## A real document

Layouts come from a handful of primitives. `Column` stacks its children with a `gap`, `Divider` draws
a line, and `Box` wraps content with a background, padding and rounded corners.

```ts
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { Document, Page, Column, Box, Text, Divider, renderToBytes } from "@jasy/pdf";

async function build() {
  const doc = Document([
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56 }, [
      Column({ gap: 12 }, [
        Text("Project Report", { size: 30, bold: true, color: "#1450aa" }),
        Text("A second look at the layout primitives.", { size: 13, color: "gray" }),
        Divider({ color: "steelblue" }),
        Box({ bg: "#1450aa11", padding: 16, radius: 8 }, [
          Text("A box with a soft background, padding and rounded corners."),
        ]),
      ]),
    ]),
  ]);

  writeFileSync("report.pdf", await renderToBytes(doc));
}

build();
```

That is the whole idea. Everything else is more of the same: more primitives, more props.

## Where to next

- **Layout** - `Column`, `Row`, `Box`, flexbox wrapping, sizing and gradients.
- **Text** - weight and colour, kerning and ligatures, hyphenation, right-to-left.
- **Pages** - headers, footers, page breaks, orphans and widows, `Page X of Y`.
- **Columns** - newspaper columns, and layouts of your own that the text flows through.
- **SVG and Canvas** - a logo that stays a vector, and a pen for everything else.
- **Forms** - fillable fields, and filling a form somebody else made.
- **Navigation** - links to the web, jumps inside the document, and a bookmark tree.
- **Tables**, **Images**, **Fonts**, **Encryption** and **Accessibility**.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/layout
Summary: Stack, space and frame your content with Column, Row, Box, Spacer and Expanded.

# Layout

Every layout is built from a handful of primitives. `Column` and `Row` stack their children, `Spacer`
and `Expanded` distribute the space between them, and `Box` and `Padding` frame and inset content.

## Column and Row

`Column` stacks its children top to bottom, `Row` left to right. Both take the same options.

```ts
Column({ gap: 12 }, [Text("First"), Text("Second")]);

Row({ gap: 8, justify: "between", align: "center" }, [
  Text("Total", { size: 16, bold: true }),
  Text("100.00 EUR"),
]);
```

| Prop             | Type                                                                 | What it does                                                      |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `gap`            | `number`                                                             | space inserted between children, in points                        |
| `justify`        | `"start" \| "center" \| "end" \| "between" \| "around"`              | distribution along the stacking axis (like CSS `justify-content`) |
| `align`          | `"start" \| "center" \| "end" \| "stretch"`                          | position across the axis (like CSS `align-items`)                 |
| `wrap`           | `boolean`                                                            | let children flow onto further lines when they do not fit         |
| `alignContent`   | `"start" \| "center" \| "end" \| "between" \| "around" \| "stretch"` | how the WRAPPED lines sit as a block                              |
| `reverse`        | `boolean`                                                            | lay the children out in the opposite order                        |
| `width` `height` | `number \| string`                                                   | fix a dimension, in points or as `"50%"` of the offered space     |

`justify: "between"` pushes the first and last child to the edges. `align: "center"` lines children up
on the cross axis. Both default to `start`.

### Wrapping, and per-child control

With `wrap`, children that do not fit start a new line, and `alignContent` places those lines as a
block. Individual children get three props of their own, on any element:

```ts
Row({ wrap: true, gap: 8, alignContent: "between" }, [
  Box({ width: "33%" }, [Text("one")]),
  Box({ width: "33%" }, [Text("two")]),
  Box({ width: "33%", order: -1 }, [Text("drawn first")]),
  Box({ flexShrink: 0 }, [Text("keeps its width, and overflows")]),
  Expanded({ flex: 1, flexBasis: 120 }, Box([Text("starts at 120pt, then grows")])),
  Box({ alignSelf: "end" }, [Text("overrides the row's align")]),
]);
```

`flexShrink` is **1**, as in CSS: when a line overflows, its children give space back in proportion to
their own width until the line fits. `0` opts a child out, so it keeps its width and runs past the edge.
An `Expanded` with a `flexBasis` takes part too, weighted by its basis - `Expanded({ flexShrink: 0 }, ...)`
keeps the basis whatever happens. A `Spacer` has no basis and gives nothing. (since beta.4)

Nothing is squeezed past what it can actually hold. A child's floor is its **min-content** extent - for
a text, its longest word - which is the same rule a browser applies through the automatic `min-width` of
a flex item. Once a child sits on its floor it stops giving, and the share it could not absorb goes to
the ones that still can.

A percentage width inside a flex line resolves against the line **minus its gaps**, so N columns at
`(100/N)%` fit exactly - CSS makes you subtract the gaps yourself.

> A layout's `align` uses the cross-axis vocabulary `start / center / end` (it is direction-agnostic -
> for a `Row` the cross axis is vertical, so `left`/`right` would not make sense). That differs from a
> [`Text`'s own `align`](/docs/pdf/text#alignment), which is `left / center / right`.

## Spacer

`Spacer` is flexible empty space. Drop one between two items and it pushes them apart.

```ts
Row([Text("Subtotal"), Spacer(), Text("100.00 EUR")]);
```

Pass a number to weight several spacers against each other: `Spacer(2)` takes twice the space of
`Spacer(1)`.

## Expanded

`Expanded` makes a child grow to fill the remaining space. Give each one a `flex` weight to share the
space in proportion.

```ts
Row({ gap: 12 }, [
  Expanded({ flex: 1 }, Box({ border: "steelblue", padding: 12, radius: 6 }, [Text("flex 1")])),
  Expanded(
    { flex: 2 },
    Box({ bg: "#1450aa11", padding: 12, radius: 6 }, [Text("flex 2, twice as wide")]),
  ),
]);
```

| Prop   | Type     | What it does                                           |
| ------ | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `flex` | `number` | the child's share of the remaining space (default `1`) |

`Expanded` makes its **child** the flex item, as CSS `flex: 1` on the child itself
(changed in beta.5):

- the child's own `width` gives way to its share;
- it never gets narrower than its content needs - a long word holds it open;
- a `maxWidth` on the child stops it growing, and the space it leaves goes to the others;
- the child lines up across the row like any item: the Row's `align`, the child's own `alignSelf`
  and `order`;
- a `%` padding on the child resolves against the Row.

Before beta.5 the child kept its own width inside its share.

`Expanded` takes a single child, not an array. In a `Row` it fills width, in a `Column` it fills height.

## Box

`Box` is the styled container: a background, a border, rounded corners, padding and an optional fixed
size. By default it fills the width it is offered (like a block element) and shrink-wraps its height to
its content. Set `width` or `height` to fix a dimension. (As a fixed child in a `Row` it shrink-wraps
its width too, since there it is not offered a width to fill.)

```ts
Box({ bg: "#1450aa11", border: "steelblue", borderWidth: 1, radius: 8, padding: 16 }, [
  Text("A framed, padded, rounded box."),
]);
```

| Prop                                                  | Type                | What it does                                            |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `bg`                                                  | `ColorInput`        | fill color                                              |
| `border`                                              | `ColorInput`        | border color (all sides)                                |
| `borderTop` `borderRight` `borderBottom` `borderLeft` | `ColorInput`        | color a single side                                     |
| `borderWidth`                                         | `number`            | border thickness (default `1` when a border is set)     |
| `radius`                                              | `number \| Corners` | corner radius - one number, or per corner               |
| `padding`                                             | `Insets`            | inner spacing (see below)                               |
| `width` `height`                                      | `number \| string`  | a fixed size in points, or `"50%"` of the offered space |
| `minWidth` `maxWidth` `minHeight` `maxHeight`         | `number \| string`  | clamp a dimension                                       |
| `aspectRatio`                                         | `number`            | derive the axis you did not pin (`16 / 9`)              |
| `overflow`                                            | `"hidden"`          | crop the children to the box, rounded corners and all   |
| `relative`                                            | `boolean`           | make this box the frame for `Positioned` children       |

### Sizing, in the order it happens

The order is the contract, and it follows CSS: **relative sizing → the aspect ratio fills whichever
axis was left open → min/max clamp.** So an explicit bound beats the ratio, the way `min-height` beats
`aspect-ratio` in a browser.

```ts
Box({ width: "50%", maxWidth: 100 }, []); // 50% of a 400pt region is 200, clamped to 100
Box({ width: 240, aspectRatio: 16 / 9 }, []); // height derived: 135
```

Percentages on `padding` and `margin` resolve against the **width** on all four sides, top and bottom
included. That is the CSS quirk, kept on purpose so a layout ported from the web behaves the same.

A `Box`'s padding takes the width the Box is **offered** - its parent's content width, as CSS takes the
containing block. (changed in beta.4) Before beta.4 it took the Box's own width, so
`Box({ width: 200, padding: "10%" })` in a 400pt column now pads 40pt, not 20pt. Inside a `Row` it takes
the Row's width (changed in beta.5) - before beta.5 it took its own there.

### Gradients

`bg` takes a gradient as readily as a color. It is written box-relative - an angle and stops - and
resolved against the box when it is drawn:

```ts
import { linearGradient, radialGradient } from "@jasy/pdf";

Box({ bg: linearGradient({ angle: 135, stops: ["#1450aa", "#7aa5e8"] }), padding: 20 }, [...]);
Box({ bg: radialGradient({ stops: ["#ffffff", "#e2483d"] }), width: 80, height: 80 }, []);
```

Angles follow CSS: `0` points up, and it turns clockwise.

### Corners, one at a time

`radius` also takes a corner object. Two radii that share an edge and would overlap are scaled down
**together**, so the shape stays smooth - react-pdf clamps each corner on its own, which pinches.

```ts
Box({ radius: { topLeft: 16, bottomRight: 16 }, bg: "#eef1f5", padding: 16 }, [...]);
```

## Padding

`Padding` insets a single child without drawing anything. It is the spacing-only cousin of `Box`.

```ts
Padding({ top: 16, bottom: 8 }, Text("Breathing room above and below."));
```

Anywhere a spacing value is taken (`padding` on a `Box`, the `Padding` element), you can write it four
ways:

```ts
16                       // all four sides
{ x: 16, y: 8 }          // horizontal / vertical
{ top: 16, left: 8 }     // per side, any subset
[16, 8, 16, 8]           // [top, right, bottom, left]
```

## Divider

`Divider` draws a thin horizontal rule across the full width of its parent - a clean separator between
sections, totals or list items.

```ts
Column({ gap: 4 }, [Text("Subtotal"), Divider(), Text("Total", { bold: true })]);
```

| Prop        | Type         | What it does                                       |
| ----------- | ------------ | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `color`     | `ColorInput` | line color (default a light gray)                  |
| `thickness` | `number`     | line thickness in points (default `1`)             |
| `margin`    | `Insets`     | space above / below the rule (default a small gap) |

```ts
Divider({ color: "#1450aa", thickness: 2, margin: { y: 12 } });
```

## One element, two places (since beta.5)

An element has one position, so placing the same one twice throws `ElementReusedError`. Place a copy:
`clone()` copies an element and everything inside it, as it was built.

```ts
const badge = Box({ bg: "#1450aa", padding: 4 }, [Text("PAID", { color: "white" })]);

Page([badge, Text("Thank you for your order."), badge.clone()]);
```

A function that builds the element (`const badge = () => Box(...)`) works just as well.

## Colors

Wherever a color is taken (`color`, `bg`, `border`), jasy accepts several forms. `rgb` and `rgba` are
small helpers you import from the package.

```ts
import { rgb, rgba } from "@jasy/pdf";

// every entry below is a valid color value:
const colors = [
  "steelblue", // any CSS color name
  "#1450aa", // hex
  "#1450aacc", // hex with alpha
  0xff1450aa, // ARGB number, alpha first
  rgb(20, 80, 170), // channels 0 to 255
  rgba(20, 80, 170, 0.5), // ... with an alpha of 0 to 1
  "rgb(20, 80, 170)", // the CSS function, as a string
  "rgb(20 80 170 / 50%)", // the modern space form, with slash-alpha
  "hsl(214, 79%, 37%)", // and hsl(), the same sRGB family
];
```

A wide-gamut function such as `color(display-p3 …)` or `light-dark()` is **named and refused** rather
than squashed into sRGB - the result would be a color nobody chose.

## See it all in one file

Here is every primitive on this page in a single document. A `Document` can hold more than one `Page`,
so each page below demonstrates one idea. Copy it, run it once, and flip through the result.

```ts
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import {
  Document,
  Page,
  Column,
  Row,
  Box,
  Padding,
  Text,
  Spacer,
  Expanded,
  Divider,
  renderToBytes,
} from "@jasy/pdf";

const heading = (t: string) => Text(t, { size: 22, bold: true, color: "#1450aa" });
const sub = (t: string) => Text(t, { size: 12, color: "gray" });

async function build() {
  const doc = Document([
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56 }, [
      Column({ gap: 16 }, [
        heading("Column and Row"),
        sub("Column stacks top to bottom, Row stacks left to right."),
        Divider({ color: "steelblue" }),
        Row({ justify: "between", align: "center" }, [
          Text("Left", { bold: true }),
          Text("Right", { bold: true }),
        ]),
      ]),
    ]),
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56 }, [
      Column({ gap: 16 }, [
        heading("Spacer"),
        sub("Flexible empty space that pushes items apart."),
        Divider({ color: "steelblue" }),
        Row([Text("Subtotal"), Spacer(), Text("100.00 EUR")]),
      ]),
    ]),
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56 }, [
      Column({ gap: 16 }, [
        heading("Expanded"),
        sub("Children grow to share the remaining space by their flex weight."),
        Divider({ color: "steelblue" }),
        Row({ gap: 12 }, [
          Expanded(
            { flex: 1 },
            Box({ border: "steelblue", padding: 14, radius: 6 }, [Text("flex 1")]),
          ),
          Expanded({ flex: 2 }, Box({ bg: "#1450aa11", padding: 14, radius: 6 }, [Text("flex 2")])),
        ]),
      ]),
    ]),
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56 }, [
      Column({ gap: 16 }, [
        heading("Box"),
        sub("A background, a border, rounded corners and padding."),
        Divider({ color: "steelblue" }),
        Box({ bg: "#1450aa11", border: "steelblue", borderWidth: 1, radius: 8, padding: 18 }, [
          Text("A framed, padded, rounded box."),
        ]),
      ]),
    ]),
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56 }, [
      Column({ gap: 16 }, [
        heading("Padding"),
        sub("Insets a single child without drawing anything."),
        Divider({ color: "steelblue" }),
        Box({ border: "steelblue", radius: 6 }, [
          Padding(
            { x: 20, y: 14 },
            Text("This text sits inside 20pt horizontal, 14pt vertical padding."),
          ),
        ]),
      ]),
    ]),
  ]);

  writeFileSync("layout-tour.pdf", await renderToBytes(doc));
}

build();
```

Run it, open `layout-tour.pdf`, and page through Column and Row, Spacer, Expanded, Box and Padding.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/text
Summary: Size, weight, color, alignment, kerning, ligatures, hyphenation and right-to-left - with Text, Paragraph and span.

# Text

`Text` puts words on the page. Pass a string and a few options, and the engine wraps it to fit the
width it is given, breaking on word boundaries using the real font metrics. You never measure anything.

## When does it wrap?

A `Text` wraps to fit the width it is given - the page content width in a `Page` or `Column`, or the
width of a `Box({ width })`, an `Expanded` or a table cell when it sits inside one. With no width limit
at all (a plain child of a `Row`), it stays on a single line, because there is nothing to wrap against.

## Styling

The second argument sets the style. Everything is optional and has a sensible default.

```ts
Text("Big and bold", { size: 26, bold: true, color: "#1450aa" });
Text("A quiet note", { size: 12, italic: true, color: "gray" });
```

| Prop            | Type                                         | What it does                                                      |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `size`          | `number`                                     | font size in points (default `12`)                                |
| `bold`          | `boolean`                                    | use the bold weight                                               |
| `italic`        | `boolean`                                    | use the italic style                                              |
| `color`         | `ColorInput`                                 | text color (any of the [color forms](/docs/pdf/layout#colors))    |
| `font`          | `string`                                     | font family (default `"Helvetica"`; see [Fonts](/docs/pdf/fonts)) |
| `align`         | `"left" \| "center" \| "right" \| "justify"` | alignment within the text block (default `"left"`)                |
| `lineHeight`    | `number`                                     | line-height multiplier; unset = the font's natural line height    |
| `underline`     | `boolean`                                    | draw an underline at the font's own position and thickness        |
| `strikethrough` | `boolean`                                    | draw a line through the text at half its x-height                 |
| `skipInk`       | `boolean`                                    | let the underline step around descenders (needs an embedded font) |
| `letterSpacing` | `number`                                     | extra space after every glyph, in points (negative tightens)      |
| `wordSpacing`   | `number`                                     | extra advance at every space, in points (CSS `word-spacing`)      |
| `textIndent`    | `number`                                     | how far the FIRST line starts in, in points                       |
| `textTransform` | `"uppercase" \| "lowercase" \| "capitalize"` | recase the text (CSS `text-transform`)                            |
| `ligatures`     | `boolean`                                    | the font's own `fi` / `fl` / `ffi` ligatures (default **on**)     |
| `breakWord`     | `boolean`                                    | split a word wider than its box, anywhere, no hyphen              |
| `hyphenate`     | `(word) => string[]`                         | split at valid points and draw the hyphen - bring your own        |
| `direction`     | `"ltr" \| "rtl"`                             | base writing direction; `rtl` starts the line on the right        |
| `maxLines`      | `number`                                     | cap the number of lines (default: unlimited)                      |
| `overflow`      | `"clip" \| "ellipsis"`                       | what to do past `maxLines` (default `"clip"`)                     |
| `orphans`       | `number`                                     | minimum lines left behind at a page break (default `2`)           |
| `widows`        | `number`                                     | minimum lines carried over to the next page (default `2`)         |

## Alignment

`align` positions the text inside its own block, independent of any surrounding layout.

```ts
Text("Centered", { align: "center" });
Text("Right aligned", { align: "right" });
Text(longParagraph, { align: "justify" });
```

`justify` spreads a line's slack over its spaces so both edges line up. The last line of a paragraph
keeps its natural spacing, as it does in print and in CSS. The engine may also **squeeze** a line
slightly - up to a quarter of a space - if that keeps one more word on it.

## Line height

`lineHeight` is a multiplier on the line spacing. Leave it unset and each line gets the font's own
**natural** line height - the same thing CSS calls `line-height: normal`, so text is comfortable to
read out of the box and capitals sit optically centered in their line. Set a number to override it:
`1` is one em (tight, capitals may just touch the edges), `1.3` to `1.5` opens body copy up further.
Whatever the value, the extra space is split evenly above and below each line.

```ts
Text("Comfortable by default - the font's natural line height.");
Text("Airier still, set once.", { lineHeight: 1.5 });
```

## Underline, strikethrough and letter spacing

Decoration and tracking read their geometry from the font itself, never a hard-coded guess.

```ts
Text("Underlined", { underline: true });
Text("Struck through", { strikethrough: true });
Text("S P A C E D  H E A D E R", { letterSpacing: 3, bold: true });
Text("tighter", { letterSpacing: -0.5 });
```

An underline sits at the position and thickness the font declares, one stroke per wrapped line, and a
struck-through line crosses at half the x-height - where a browser puts it. `letterSpacing` adds a
fixed gap after every glyph (a negative value tightens); it is counted in wrapping and alignment, so
spaced text still breaks and aligns correctly. All of these also work on a single [`span`](#mixed-styles-in-one-line)
and cascade from `Document` / `DefaultTextStyle`.

`skipInk` lets the underline break around descenders like a browser does - it needs an embedded font
(the standard PDF fonts keep their outlines in the viewer, not in the document), and asking for it
with a standard font is an error rather than a silent no-op.

## Kerning and ligatures

Both are **on by default**, because the font's designer drew them and nobody should need to know the
words to get text set properly.

**Kerning** applies the font's own pair adjustments, tightening combinations like `AV`, `To` and `Wa`
so headings read the way they do on the web instead of falling into loose slabs. It works for the
standard fonts and for embedded ones (the legacy `kern` table and modern OpenType `GPOS` alike).

**Ligatures** merge `fi`, `fl` and `ffi` into the single glyph the font provides, read from its
`GSUB` table. Embedded fonts only - the standard 14 have no such table.

```ts
Text("office affluent film"); // ffi and fl become one glyph each
Text("office affluent film", { ligatures: false }); // opt out for this text

await renderToBytes(doc, { kerning: false }); // or turn kerning off document-wide
```

`ligatures` is an inheritable text style, so it can be set on `Document`, on a `DefaultTextStyle`
subtree, or on one `Text`.

## A word that does not fit

By default a word wider than its box **overflows**, exactly as it does in CSS. Two layers stack on top
of that, and neither is on unless you ask:

```ts
Text(email, { breakWord: true }); // split where the box ends, no hyphen
Text(german, { hyphenate }); // split at valid points, with a hyphen
```

`breakWord` is the floor: an e-mail address, an IBAN or an invoice number has no valid hyphenation
point anywhere, and it is what stops a mandatory field on an invoice from being drawn across its own
label.

`hyphenate` is a **hook**, not bundled data. Give it a function that returns a word's parts, and jasy
draws the hyphen at the break. Any pattern library will do:

```ts
import { hyphenateSync } from "hyphen/de";
const hyphenate = (word: string) => hyphenateSync(word).split("\u00AD");

Text("Rechtsschutzversicherungsgesellschaften", { hyphenate, breakWord: true });
```

No pattern data ships in `@jasy/pdf`: German alone is 732 KB, and hyphenating without being told the
language is worse than not hyphenating at all. The default is a position, not an omission - _we do not
hyphenate until you name the language._

## Right to left, and Arabic

Set `direction: "rtl"` and the line starts on the right. Mixed text is reordered per Unicode UAX #9
either way, so Hebrew inside an English paragraph already comes out right without the flag - what the
flag decides is where the LINE begins.

```ts
Text("שלום world", { direction: "rtl" });
Text("مرحبا بالعالم", { font: "Amiri", direction: "rtl" });
```

Arabic letters **join**, read from the font's own `GSUB`, and lam-alef collapses into one glyph. That
needs an embedded Arabic face; copied text comes back as real Arabic, not as presentation forms.

## Line breaks

A `\n` in your string is a **hard break**: it breaks the line even where there is room, because it is
an instruction rather than wrapping. `\r\n` and a lone `\r` mean the same thing, a tab becomes a space,
and invisible control characters are dropped - except the ones that do work, like the zero-width
joiner Arabic shaping needs.

## Inheriting text styles

Every option above has a built-in default, but you rarely want to repeat `size` or `color` on every
line. Set them **once** and let them cascade - exactly like CSS, or Flutter's `DefaultTextStyle`.

### Document-wide defaults

Pass the text options to `Document` and every `Text` inherits them unless it sets its own. This is the
cleanest way to give a whole document one consistent typeface, size, color and rhythm.

```ts
Document({ font: "Times-Roman", size: 11, color: "#1f2a37", lineHeight: 1.5 }, [
  Page({ size: "A4" }, [
    Text("Inherits the serif, 11pt, dark ink and 1.5 line-height."),
    Text("Sets nothing either - identical to the line above."),
    Text("Overrides just the color; size, font and line-height still inherit.", {
      color: "#c0392b",
    }),
  ]),
]);
```

### A font that covers what the first one cannot

`font` also takes a **list**. Each code point is drawn by the first family in it that has a glyph for
that character, so mixed-script text works without splitting it by hand:

```ts
Text("Hello 你好 مرحبا", { font: ["Inter", "NotoSansCJK", "Amiri"] });
```

A code point no family in the stack can draw is removed and **reported** rather than emitted as a
`.notdef` box - PDF/A forbids referencing one. `renderToBytes(doc, { onMissingGlyphs })` tells you
exactly which characters went missing, so a lost tick mark never silently stops an invoice.

### A default for one section - `DefaultTextStyle`

To re-default a _section_ instead of the whole document, wrap it in `DefaultTextStyle`. Its children
inherit the new values, layered onto whatever was already inherited from above.

```ts
DefaultTextStyle({ size: 9, color: "gray" }, [
  Text("Small and grey - a footnote, a caption, a contact block."),
  Text("Same here, nothing set on it."),
  Text("Still 9pt, but overrides the color.", { color: "#1450aa" }),
]);
```

To style one whole page, make it the page's child: `Page([ DefaultTextStyle({ … }, [ …content ]) ])`.

### How a value is resolved

For each property the most specific source wins - and _only_ that property; the rest keep inheriting
(a per-property merge, like Flutter):

```
explicit on the Text  >  nearest DefaultTextStyle  >  Document defaults  >  built-in default
```

Only **text** properties inherit - `font`, `size`, `color`, `bold`, `italic`, `align`, `lineHeight`,
the same set CSS inherits. Box and layout properties (padding, border, width, background) never do.

## Truncating long text

By default a `Text` wraps onto as many lines as it needs. Cap it with `maxLines`, and choose what
happens to the overflow with `overflow`: `"clip"` cuts hard, `"ellipsis"` ends the last line with
`...`. Truncation needs a bounded width - a `Column`, a `Box({ width })`, an `Expanded` or a table cell.

```ts
Box({ width: 220 }, [
  Text("Premium Wireless Noise-Cancelling Over-Ear Headphones with 40 Hour Battery Life", {
    maxLines: 2,
    overflow: "ellipsis",
  }),
]);
```

`maxLines: 1` clamps to a single line - handy for a long product name in a narrow table cell.

## Mixed styles in one line

To change style partway through a line, pass an array of `span(...)` runs instead of a string. Each
`span` overrides only the fields it sets, inheriting the rest from the `Text` options.

```ts
import { Text, span } from "@jasy/pdf";

Text(
  [
    span("This line mixes "),
    span("bold", { bold: true }),
    span(", "),
    span("italic", { italic: true }),
    span(" and "),
    span("color", { color: "#1450aa", bold: true }),
    span(" in one run."),
  ],
  { size: 14 },
);
```

`span` takes every style that belongs to a run (changed in beta.5) - size, font, weight, color,
decoration and `skipInk`, `letterSpacing`, `wordSpacing`, `textTransform`, `ligatures`, `breakWord`,
`hyphenate`. A style set on a span wins over the `Text`; one left unset inherits. What belongs to the
whole block stays on the `Text`: `align`, `lineHeight`, `maxLines`, `direction` and `textIndent`.
Before beta.5 a span accepted `direction` and `textIndent` and did nothing with them, and dropped
several of the run styles. It adds two of its own:

```ts
Text([span("Total 1.190,00 EUR"), span("1", { verticalAlign: "super", size: 7 })]);
Text([span("Read the "), span("terms", { href: "https://example.com/terms" }), span(".")]);
```

`verticalAlign: "super" | "sub"` raises a footnote marker or lowers an index - it shifts the baseline
only, so pass a smaller `size` too if you want the browser's `<sup>` look. And `href` / `to` link just
that run rather than the whole text.

A word that runs across two spans breaks with `breakWord` where Chrome breaks it: the line is filled
first, and a break after a character is allowed by that character's span. `hyphenate` is still asked
for each span's piece of such a word, not the whole word
([#113](https://github.com/jasy-pdf/jasy/issues/113)).

## Paragraphs

`Paragraph` is `Text` with a different name. It behaves identically, but reads as intent when you mean
a block of body copy rather than a label or a heading.

```ts
Paragraph(
  "Long text wraps automatically to fit its width, breaking on word boundaries using the real " +
    "font metrics, so you never have to measure anything yourself.",
  { size: 12 },
);
```

## See it all in one file

Copy this, run it with `npx tsx text-demo.ts`, and open `text.pdf`.

```ts
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { Document, Page, Column, Text, Paragraph, span, Divider, renderToBytes } from "@jasy/pdf";

async function build() {
  const doc = Document([
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56 }, [
      Column({ gap: 12 }, [
        Text("Big and bold", { size: 26, bold: true, color: "#1450aa" }),
        Text("Italic and gray", { size: 14, italic: true, color: "gray" }),
        Text("Centered", { size: 14, align: "center" }),
        Text("Right aligned", { size: 14, align: "right" }),
        Divider({ color: "steelblue" }),
        Text(
          [
            span("This line mixes "),
            span("bold", { bold: true }),
            span(", "),
            span("italic", { italic: true }),
            span(" and "),
            span("color", { color: "#1450aa", bold: true }),
            span(" in one run."),
          ],
          { size: 14 },
        ),
        Divider({ color: "steelblue" }),
        Paragraph(
          "Paragraph is Text with a name that reads as intent. Long text wraps automatically to fit " +
            "its width, breaking on word boundaries using the real font metrics, so you never measure " +
            "anything yourself.",
          { size: 12 },
        ),
      ]),
    ]),
  ]);

  writeFileSync("text.pdf", await renderToBytes(doc));
}

build();
```

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/tables
Summary: Lay out rows and columns with repeating headers, flexible widths and clean rules - the heart of any invoice.

# Tables

A `Table` is the heart of most invoices and reports. You give it the column widths and the rows, and
it aligns every cell, repeats the header across pages, and breaks between rows so a row never gets cut
in half.

```ts
import { Table, Text } from "@jasy/pdf";

Table(
  {
    columns: ["1fr", 50, 80, 90],
    header: [
      Text("Description", { bold: true }),
      Text("Qty", { bold: true, align: "right" }),
      Text("Unit", { bold: true, align: "right" }),
      Text("Amount", { bold: true, align: "right" }),
    ],
    cellPadding: { x: 8, y: 6 },
    rule: "#c2ccdb",
  },
  [
    [
      Text("Website design & build"),
      Text("1", { align: "right" }),
      Text("9600.00", { align: "right" }),
      Text("9600.00", { align: "right" }),
    ],
    [
      Text("Strategy consulting"),
      Text("12", { align: "right" }),
      Text("140.00", { align: "right" }),
      Text("1680.00", { align: "right" }),
    ],
  ],
);
```

## Columns

`columns` has one entry per column, and decides how wide each one is. Mix the three kinds freely.

| Width                | Meaning                                                                                       |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `90`                 | a fixed width in points                                                                       |
| `"1fr"`, `"2fr"`     | a fraction of the leftover space, shared in proportion (like CSS `fr`)                        |
| `"auto"`             | as wide as the widest cell in that column, measured at layout time                            |
| `"minmax(40, auto)"` | like `"auto"`, but never narrower than 40pt - a column that may stay empty (since beta.4) |

A typical invoice uses one `"1fr"` description column that absorbs the slack, and fixed-width number
columns on the right.

## Cells and rows

`rows` is an array of rows, each an array of cells. A cell is any element, or a plain string (which is
wrapped in `Text` for you). Right-align number columns with `Text(value, { align: "right" })`.

```ts
[
  ["Apples", "Granny Smith", Text("12", { align: "right" })],
  ["Oranges", "Valencia", Text("8", { align: "right" })],
];
```

## Options

| Prop              | Type            | What it does                                                             |
| ----------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `columns`         | `ColumnWidth[]` | one width per column (required)                                          |
| `header`          | `Cell[]`        | a header row that repeats at the top of every page the table spills onto |
| `cellPadding`     | `Insets`        | padding inside every cell                                                |
| `rule`            | `ColorInput`    | a thin horizontal line under the header and along the foot               |
| `cellBorder`      | `ColorInput`    | a full grid line around every cell                                       |
| `gap`             | `number`        | space between rows and columns                                           |
| `rowGap` `colGap` | `number`        | override `gap` for one axis                                              |

## Rules or a full grid

`rule` draws two thin lines, under the header and at the foot - the clean look most invoices use.
`cellBorder` instead draws the complete grid around every cell.

```ts
// invoice style: thin separators
{ columns: ["1fr", 80], rule: "#c2ccdb", cellPadding: { x: 8, y: 6 } }

// spreadsheet style: full grid
{ columns: ["1fr", 80], cellBorder: "#c2ccdb", cellPadding: 8 }
```

Use one or the other. `cellBorder` already draws the outer edges, so do not wrap the table in a
`Box` border as well, or the edges double up.

## Across pages

A `Table` is just a `Column` of atomic rows, so it paginates for free: when a row does not fit on the
current page it moves to the next one whole, and the `header` row reprints at the top. You write the
rows once and long tables simply flow.

## See it all in one file

```ts
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { Document, Page, Table, Text, renderToBytes } from "@jasy/pdf";

const money = (n: number) => Text(n.toFixed(2), { align: "right" });

async function build() {
  const doc = Document([
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56 }, [
      Table(
        {
          columns: ["1fr", 50, 80, 90],
          header: [
            Text("Description", { bold: true }),
            Text("Qty", { bold: true, align: "right" }),
            Text("Unit", { bold: true, align: "right" }),
            Text("Amount", { bold: true, align: "right" }),
          ],
          cellPadding: { x: 8, y: 6 },
          rule: "#c2ccdb",
        },
        [
          [Text("Website design & build"), Text("1", { align: "right" }), money(9600), money(9600)],
          [Text("Strategy consulting"), Text("12", { align: "right" }), money(140), money(1680)],
          [Text("Printed brand book"), Text("25", { align: "right" }), money(28), money(700)],
        ],
      ),
    ]),
  ]);

  writeFileSync("table.pdf", await renderToBytes(doc));
}

build();
```

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/images
Summary: Place PNG and JPEG images at their own size or in a box, with object-fit scaling, alignment and rounded corners.

# Images

`Image` places a raster image, PNG or JPEG. Give it a source, and optionally a size.

```ts
import { Image } from "@jasy/pdf";

Image("logo.png", { width: 120 });
```

Hand it an **SVG** and it stays a vector instead of becoming a bitmap - same call, no flag:

```ts
Image("logo.svg", { width: 120 });
```

See [SVG and Canvas](/docs/pdf/drawing) for what that path covers.

## Sources

| Source                 | Example                                 |                                         |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| a file path            | `Image("logo.png")`                     | Node only - the browser has no paths    |
| a URL                  | `Image("https://example.com/logo.png")` | `http(s):` and `data:`, fetched (below) |
| the bytes              | `Image(bytes)`                          | a `Uint8Array` - an upload, a `fetch()` |
| your own `CustomImage` | `Image(myImage)`                        | any other source you load yourself      |

What the image is comes from its bytes, never from its name, so `.../photo?id=7` works. A file is read
when you call `Image`, so a wrong path fails on that line, not later in the render.

- **PNG** keeps its transparency.
- **JPEG** keeps the color space it was saved in: gray, RGB or CMYK. A photo's EXIF orientation is
  applied, so a phone picture stands upright, as it does in a browser.

## From a URL (since beta.4)

An `http(s):` or `data:` address works wherever a file path does - PNG, JPEG and SVG alike:

```ts
Image("https://example.com/logo.png", { width: 120 });
Image("https://example.com/logo.svg", { width: 120 }); // still a vector
```

The image is fetched once per render, before layout, so a width-only image still gets its height from
the real aspect ratio. A dead link fails with an `ImageUrlError` that names the address - it is never
silently left out. Each fetch has a 15 s timeout and a 32 MB ceiling, enforced while the bytes arrive.

A URL image that is first created inside a `PageBuilder` cannot be fetched before layout. Give it a
`width` and a `height`; without them it fills the space it is offered and reports `image-unsized` (see
[Output](/docs/pdf/output)).

## Size (changed in beta.5)

With **no size**, an image is as large as its file says: its pixels at the resolution the file declares
(a PNG's `pHYs`, a JPEG's JFIF or EXIF), else at 96 dpi - a CSS pixel. A 240 px logo without a
declaration is 180 pt wide; a 144 dpi screenshot comes out at half its pixel count. Wider than the
space it is offered, it is scaled down to fit, keeping its ratio. It is never scaled up.

Before beta.5 a pixel was a point, and the resolution in the file was ignored.

```ts
Image("logo.png"); // its own size, scaled down to fit
Image("logo.png", { width: 120 }); // the height follows the ratio
Image("banner.png", { width: "100%" }); // the full width it is offered
Image("photo.jpg", { width: 160, height: 100, fit: "cover" }); // a box of its own
```

Give **one side** and the other follows the image's ratio. A size is points or a percentage of the
space offered. `aspectRatio` replaces the image's own ratio, and `minWidth` / `maxWidth` / `minHeight`
/ `maxHeight` clamp the result, as on any element (see [Layout](/docs/pdf/layout)).

## Fitting the box

`fit` controls how the image fills its box. It mirrors CSS `object-fit`.

| `fit`       | What it does                                                     |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"fill"`    | stretched to the box exactly (the default) - may distort         |
| `"contain"` | scaled to fit inside the box, whole image visible, may letterbox |
| `"cover"`   | scaled to fill the box, cut at the edges, no distortion          |
| `"none"`    | its own size, not scaled, cut at the edges of the box            |

Without a size the box is derived from the image, so the default `"fill"` draws it undistorted. With
both `width` and `height`, pick the `fit` you want.

## Where it sits in its box (since beta.5)

When `fit` leaves room or cuts the image, `align` says where it sits. The default is `"center"`.

```ts
Image("portrait.jpg", { width: 120, height: 120, fit: "cover", align: "top" }); // keeps the face
```

`align` is `"center"`, `"top"`, `"bottom"`, `"left"`, `"right"`, `"top left"`, `"top right"`,
`"bottom left"` or `"bottom right"`.

Where the image's box sits in its Column or Row is the parent's `align`, or the image's own
`alignSelf` - as for any element.

## Rounded and circular

`radius` rounds the image box (the image is clipped to the rounded rect). A square image with a radius
of half its side becomes a circle, perfect for an avatar.

```ts
Image("avatar.jpg", { width: 96, height: 96, fit: "cover", radius: 48 });
Image("photo.jpg", { width: 160, height: 100, fit: "cover", radius: [12, 12, 0, 0] }); // top only
```

One number rounds all four corners. An object names them (`{ topLeft, topRight, bottomRight,
bottomLeft }`); an array is CSS order, clockwise from the top left.

## Options

| Option                                        | Type                                       | What it does                                                                                              |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `width` `height`                              | `number \| "50%"`                          | the size, in points or a percentage of the space offered                                                  |
| `fit`                                         | `"fill" \| "contain" \| "cover" \| "none"` | how the image fills its box (default `"fill"`)                                                            |
| `align` (since beta.5)                    | see above                                  | where the image sits in its box (default `"center"`)                                                      |
| `radius`                                      | `number \| object \| [tl, tr, br, bl]`     | rounds the image box                                                                                      |
| `alt`                                         | `string`                                   | alternate text - in a [tagged PDF](/docs/pdf/accessibility) the image is a figure; without it, decoration |
| `aspectRatio`                                 | `number`                                   | width / height, replacing the image's own ratio                                                           |
| `minWidth` `maxWidth` `minHeight` `maxHeight` | `number \| "50%"`                          | clamp the size                                                                                            |
| `alignSelf` `order` `flexShrink`              |                                            | its place in a Column or Row, as on any element ([Layout](/docs/pdf/layout))                              |

An SVG through `Image` takes the size and layout options and `alt`. A `fit` other than `"contain"`,
`align` and `radius` are a named error there: a drawing is always scaled to fit and centered, which is
SVG's own default.

## What it refuses

Nothing is silently dropped or drawn wrong. Each of these stops the render with an error that says what
to do:

- a file that cannot be read, a URL that cannot be fetched (`ImageUrlError`), or a format other than
  PNG, JPEG and SVG;
- a JPEG that PDF viewers cannot decode - lossless, hierarchical or arithmetic-coded (`JpegFormatError`);
- a CMYK JPEG in a PDF/A document, whose sRGB output intent forbids CMYK (`JpegFormatError`) - convert
  the image to RGB first.

## See it all in one file

Copy this next to an image named `photo.png` and run it with `npx tsx images.ts`.

```ts
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { Document, Page, Row, Column, Text, Image, renderToBytes } from "@jasy/pdf";

async function build() {
  const doc = Document([
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56 }, [
      Column({ gap: 16 }, [
        Text("Images", { size: 22, bold: true, color: "#1450aa" }),
        Image("photo.png", { width: 200 }),
        Row({ gap: 16 }, [
          Image("photo.png", { width: 120, height: 90, fit: "contain" }),
          Image("photo.png", { width: 120, height: 90, fit: "cover", align: "top" }),
          Image("photo.png", { width: 90, height: 90, fit: "cover", radius: 45 }),
        ]),
      ]),
    ]),
  ]);

  writeFileSync("images.pdf", await renderToBytes(doc));
}

build();
```

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/fonts
Summary: The 14 standard fonts out of the box, plus embed your own from a file, bytes or a URL - .ttf, .woff and .woff2 alike.

# Fonts

Out of the box you have the 14 standard PDF fonts, no setup required. Bring your own TrueType font when
you need brand type or characters beyond Latin, and jasy embeds it, subsets it and compresses it for
you.

## The standard fonts

Three families ship with every PDF reader, so jasy embeds nothing for them. Pick one with `font`; the
default is Helvetica. `bold` and `italic` select the matching face.

```ts
Text("Helvetica is the default");
Text("A serif heading", { font: "Times-Roman", bold: true });
Text("Monospaced code", { font: "Courier" });
```

The family names are `Helvetica`, `Times-Roman` and `Courier`. They cover Latin text (Windows-1252),
including the Euro sign and accented characters.

## Embedding your own font

Register a font on the document with `addFont(name, source)`, then use that name as `font` on any
`Text`. The source is a path (jasy reads it on Node), the raw bytes, or a per-style family - and the
container does not matter: **`.ttf`, `.woff` and `.woff2` are the same thing at the call site.**

```ts
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { Document, Page, Column, Text, renderToBytes } from "@jasy/pdf";

async function build() {
  const doc = Document([
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56 }, [
      Column({ gap: 10 }, [
        Text("Set in Inter", { font: "Inter", size: 22 }),
        Text("Full Unicode too: Привет, Γειά, čeština", { font: "Inter" }),
      ]),
    ]),
  ]);

  doc.addFont("Inter", "Inter-Regular.ttf"); // a path - jasy reads it

  writeFileSync("typed.pdf", await renderToBytes(doc));
}

build();
```

The name is what you pass to `Text({ font })`. A custom font also unlocks full Unicode (Cyrillic,
Greek, Latin Extended), which the standard fonts cannot show - and, because it carries its own
OpenType tables, it brings **kerning** and **Latin ligatures** with it (both on by default) and makes
Arabic shaping and skip-ink underlines possible. See [Text](/docs/pdf/text).

Already hold the bytes (say, a browser upload)? Pass them instead of a path:

```ts
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
doc.addFont("Inter", readFileSync("Inter-Regular.ttf"));
```

### From a URL

`addFontFromUrl` fetches it for you - the one form that also works in the browser, where there is no
filesystem to point at. It resolves **at registration**, exactly as `addFont` reads a path there and
then, so a dead link fails on the line that asked for the font rather than inside a later render.

```ts
await doc.addFontFromUrl("Inter", "https://example.com/Inter-Regular.woff2");

// a whole family in one call - the files are fetched in parallel
await doc.addFontFromUrl("Inter", {
  normal: "https://example.com/Inter-Regular.woff2",
  bold: "https://example.com/Inter-Bold.woff2",
});
```

It is guarded like any other network read: a 15 second timeout, a 32 MB ceiling enforced while the
body arrives, and every failure wrapped as a `FontUrlError` that says what the file actually was - a
404 HTML page is reported as such, not as a broken font table.

In a bundler, `import url from "./Inter.woff2?url"` gives you exactly the URL this wants. That is the
whole browser story: an import and one line.

### Managing the registry

The document owns its fonts, so you can ask it what is registered - and you never have to deregister:

```ts
doc.getFonts(); // ["Inter"]  - the registered names
doc.hasFont("Inter"); // true
doc.addFont("Inter", "..."); // re-adding a name overwrites it
```

A font you register but never use on a `Text` is **dropped at render and costs nothing**. Register
freely; only the faces you actually use are embedded.

## Bold, italic and a whole family

Register the faces of a family under one name and jasy picks the right one for `bold` / `italic`. A
requested style you did not register falls back to the family's regular face, cleanly.

```ts
doc.addFont("Inter", {
  normal: "Inter-Regular.ttf",
  bold: "Inter-Bold.ttf",
  italic: "Inter-Italic.ttf",
  boldItalic: "Inter-BoldItalic.ttf",
});
```

```ts
Text("Bold Inter", { font: "Inter", bold: true });
Text("Italic Inter", { font: "Inter", italic: true });
```

Only `normal` is required; add `bold` / `italic` / `boldItalic` as you have them, each a path or bytes.

## What jasy does for you

- **Subsetting** - only the glyphs you use are embedded (a 740 KB font drops to tens of KB).
- **Compression** - the embedded program is FlateDecode-compressed.
- **Copy and search** - a `ToUnicode` map ships with the font, so the text stays selectable and
  searchable in the reader.

## Which files jasy reads

| Format                                             | Supported                       |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `.ttf` (TrueType, and TrueType-flavoured OpenType) | yes                             |
| `.woff`                                            | yes - unwrapped for you         |
| `.woff2`                                           | yes - unwrapped for you         |
| `.otf` with CFF outlines                           | not yet, and it says so by name |

A WOFF is the same font behind a small wrapper; a **WOFF2** is more than that - it does not merely
compress the glyph table, it rewrites it, with the points spread across five separate streams. jasy
unpacks both itself. The only dependency in that path is a Brotli decoder, and it is loaded **only if
a WOFF2 actually turns up**, so a document without one never pays for it.

The reconstruction is checked against the source rather than assumed: all 6,253 glyph outlines of a
real font come back identical, and the rendered page is pixel-for-pixel the same as the one produced
from its `.ttf`.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/pages
Summary: Page size, orientation and margins, repeating headers and footers, page numbers, automatic pagination, and page-break control (PageBreak, breakBefore/After, keepTogether).

# Pages

A `Document` holds one or more `Page`s. Each page sets its own size, orientation and margins, and when
its content is taller than the page, jasy flows it onto as many pages as it needs, on its own.

```ts
Page({ size: "A4", orientation: "portrait", margin: 56 }, [Text("One page.")]);
```

| Prop          | Type                                         | What it does                                   |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `size`        | `PageSize` or a name like `"A4"`, `"letter"` | the page format (default A4)                   |
| `orientation` | `"portrait" \| "landscape"`                  | rotates the format (default portrait)          |
| `margin`      | `Insets`                                     | the content box inset (default 56pt all sides) |
| `header`      | an element                                   | drawn at the top of every page                 |
| `footer`      | an element                                   | drawn at the bottom of every page              |

A `Page` also takes the [`Column` options](/docs/pdf/layout) (`gap`, `justify`, `align`), since its
children are stacked in a column.

### A size of your own

Not every document is A-something. A label, a ticket or a shelf tag gets its measurements directly -
in points, or in millimetres with the `mm` helper:

```ts
import { mm } from "@jasy/pdf";

Page({ size: mm(50, 65), margin: 4 }, [Text("A 50 x 65 mm label")]);
Page({ size: { width: 200, height: 120 }, margin: 8 }, [Text("200 x 120 points")]);
```

Everything else follows: the page box, the content box and the coordinate flip all use the size you
gave, so headers, footers and pagination behave exactly as on a named format.

## Many pages

Hand `Document` a list of pages. Each can differ, mixing sizes and orientations freely.

```ts
Document([
  Page({ size: "A4" }, [Text("Cover")]),
  Page({ size: "A5", orientation: "landscape" }, [Text("A landscape insert")]),
]);
```

## Headers, footers and pagination

A `header` and `footer` are laid out once and reprinted on every page the content spills onto, so a long
table or a long stack of paragraphs keeps its letterhead and page furniture throughout. You write the
content once; jasy paginates.

```ts
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { Document, Page, Column, Row, Text, renderToBytes } from "@jasy/pdf";

const header = Row({ justify: "between" }, [
  Text("Acme Inc.", { bold: true, color: "#1450aa" }),
  Text("Report"),
]);
const footer = Row({ justify: "between" }, [
  Text("Confidential", { size: 9, color: "gray" }),
  Text("2026", { size: 9, color: "gray" }),
]);

async function build() {
  const body = Array.from({ length: 60 }, (_, i) =>
    Text(`Paragraph ${i + 1} - long body text that flows across pages.`, { size: 12 }),
  );

  const doc = Document([
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56, header, footer }, [Column({ gap: 6 }, body)]),
  ]);

  writeFileSync("report.pdf", await renderToBytes(doc));
}

build();
```

The 60 paragraphs are taller than one page, so the result is several pages, each carrying the same
header and footer.

## Page breaks

jasy paginates on its own, but sometimes you want to decide where a break falls - start a section on a
fresh page, or stop a block from being cut in half at the boundary. These mirror the CSS
`break-before` / `break-after` / `break-inside` properties.

### Force a new page

`PageBreak()` sends everything after it to a fresh page, no matter how much room is left.

```ts
import { Document, Page, Column, Text, PageBreak } from "@jasy/pdf";

Column([Text("Chapter one ends here."), PageBreak(), Text("Chapter two starts on a new page.")]);
```

### Break before or after an element

The same thing as a prop - put `breakBefore` or `breakAfter` on any `Box`, `Column` or `Row`
(CSS `break-before` / `break-after: page`):

```ts
Column([
  Text("Summary"),
  Box({ breakBefore: true, padding: 12 }, [Text("Appendix - always starts its own page")]),
]);
```

A `breakBefore` at the very top of a page is ignored, so you never get a stray blank page.

### Keep a block together

`keepTogether` refuses to split a group across a page boundary (CSS `break-inside: avoid`). If the group
does not fit in the space left but would fit on a fresh page, it moves there whole; if it is taller than
a whole page, it splits anyway, so pagination always finishes. Nesting works - an inner `keepTogether`
still holds even when an outer one has to give.

```ts
import { keepTogether } from "@jasy/pdf";

keepTogether([
  Text("Invoice total", { bold: true }),
  Divider(),
  Text("Subtotal    100.00"),
  Text("Tax          19.00"),
  Text("Total       119.00", { bold: true }),
]);
// or as a prop: Box({ keepTogether: true, padding: 12 }, [ /* ... */ ])
```

All four are available in `@jasy/vue` and `@jasy/nuxt` as well: `<PageBreak />`, `<KeepTogether>`, and
the `break-before` / `break-after` / `keep-together` props. In `@jasy/react` they are `<PageBreak />`,
`<KeepTogether>` and `breakBefore` / `breakAfter` / `keepTogether`.

## Orphans and widows

An orphan is the first line of a paragraph left alone at the foot of a page; a widow is the last line
pushed alone to the top of the next. jasy honours both, with CSS's own defaults of **2**:

```ts
Text(longParagraph, { orphans: 3, widows: 3 });
Text(longParagraph, { orphans: 1, widows: 1 }); // switch the protection off
```

Each is a whole number of lines, at least 1 - anything else is refused by name. Unlike in CSS they do
**not** inherit: a break rule is set per paragraph. (Browser support is uneven here - Chrome honours
them in paged media, Firefox never implemented them - which is exactly why a PDF engine has to do it
itself.)

## Page numbers

`PageNumber()` and `PageCount()` print the current page and the document total. Drop them wherever you
like - a footer is the usual home, but nothing stops you putting them in the body, in a table cell, or
five times on one page.

```ts
Page(
  { footer: Row({ justify: "center" }, [Text("Page "), PageNumber(), Text(" of "), PageCount()]) },
  [Column(body)],
);
```

Both take the usual [`Text` options](/docs/pdf/text) plus an `offset`, which is added to the number. Use
it when a cover page should not count:

```ts
PageNumber({ offset: -1, size: 9, color: "gray" });
```

### Numbering within one section

A long `Page` that flows onto several sheets can number itself as well as the document.
`SubPageNumber()` and `SubPageCount()` count **within that one logical page**, so an invoice plus its
attachment can foot "Attachment, page 1 of 2" next to "sheet 3 of 4":

```ts
Row({ justify: "between" }, [
  Row({}, [Text("Page "), PageNumber(), Text(" of "), PageCount()]),
  Row({}, [Text("Sheet "), SubPageNumber(), Text(" of "), SubPageCount()]),
]);
```

### Building your own

Behind both sits one primitive: `PageBuilder`. It hands you the page's facts and draws whatever you
return, so formatting and conditions are plain JavaScript.

```ts
import { Document, Page, Column, Row, Text, PageBuilder } from "@jasy/pdf";

const doc = Document([
  Page(
    {
      // A full title on page 1, a quiet continuation line afterwards.
      header: PageBuilder(({ pageNumber }) =>
        pageNumber === 1
          ? Text("Acme Inc. - Annual Report", { size: 16, bold: true })
          : Text("Annual Report (continued)", { size: 9, color: "gray" }),
      ),
      footer: PageBuilder(({ pageNumber, pageCount }) =>
        Text(`Page ${pageNumber} of ${pageCount}`, { size: 9, align: "center" }),
      ),
    },
    [Column(body)],
  ),
]);
```

The closure receives `pageNumber` (1-based, counting **physical** pages, so a `Page` that overflows
contributes several), `pageCount` (the document total) and `pageSize` (the media box in points). In
`@jasy/react`, `<PageBuilder>` takes this function as its child - see
[Components](/docs/react/components#page-numbers).

Getting `pageCount` right is why jasy paginates the whole document before it draws anything: the total
has to exist before page 1 is painted. That ordering leaves two things worth knowing, and they follow
from the same chicken-and-egg - the content decides the count that the content displays.

> A conditional header may **shrink** on later pages, never **grow**. The body band is measured against
> the first build, so a taller header on page 3 would squeeze the body it was already sized for.
> Shrinking only frees up room, which is harmless.

Inside the flowing body the box is reserved before the total is known, so a much wider final string
(`"9 of 10"` where `"1 of 1"` was measured) can paint slightly past it. Keep dynamic body content roughly
constant in width. In a header or footer the numbers are always exact.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/columns
Summary: Newspaper columns with SplitView, your own column layouts with Flow and Region, ColumnBreak, and columns that balance on the last page.

# Columns (since beta.5)

Text that runs down one column and continues in the next, then on the next page. `SplitView` is the
ready-made newspaper. `Flow` and `Region` build any other layout: a title area, a sidebar, columns of
different widths.

Everything inside paginates as it does on a page. A paragraph splits at its lines, a table repeats its
header, `keepTogether` holds, orphans and widows count.

::callout{type="warning"}
Experimental: the shape of these components may still change before 1.0.
::

## Newspaper columns

```ts
import { Document, Page, Text, SplitView } from "@jasy/pdf";

Document([
  Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56, gap: 12 }, [
    Text("The Valley Courier", { size: 28, bold: true, color: "#1450aa" }),
    SplitView({ columns: 3, colGap: 16, rowGap: 8 }, paragraphs),
    Text("This line follows the columns, right where they end.", { italic: true }),
  ]),
]);
```

The content fills the first column, then the next, then the next page. On its last page the columns
balance: they come out about equally tall, as CSS columns do, and what follows sits right below them.

| Option    | Default | What it does                                                            |
| --------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `columns` | `2`     | how many columns, side by side and equally wide                         |
| `gap`     | `0`     | space between the columns and between the content's elements            |
| `colGap`  | `gap`   | space between the columns                                               |
| `rowGap`  | `gap`   | space between the content's elements                                    |
| `balance` | `true`  | equal columns on the last page; `false` fills one column, then the next |

## Breaking to the next column

`ColumnBreak()` starts the next column. From the last column, it starts the first one on the next page.

```ts
SplitView({ columns: 2, gap: 16 }, [
  Text("Summary", { bold: true }),
  Text(summary),
  ColumnBreak(),
  Text("Details", { bold: true }),
  Text(details),
]);
```

A `ColumnBreak` outside a column (in a `Row`, a table row, or no column at all) does nothing, and
reports it once as `column-break-ignored`. To start a new page, use `PageBreak`.

## A layout of your own

`Flow` takes a `template`: a function that builds one page of the layout. Put a `Region` wherever the
content should go. The content fills the Regions in the order they appear, then continues on the next
page with a fresh template.

```ts
import { Document, Page, Column, Row, Box, Text, Expanded, Flow, Region } from "@jasy/pdf";

Document([
  Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56 }, [
    Flow(
      {
        gap: 8,
        template: ({ index }) =>
          Column({ gap: 12 }, [
            index === 0
              ? Text("Annual Report", { size: 22, bold: true, color: "#1450aa" })
              : Text("Annual Report, continued", { size: 9, italic: true, color: "gray" }),
            Row({ gap: 16 }, [
              Expanded(Region()),
              Box({ bg: "#f3f5f9", padding: 8 }, [Region({ width: 150 })]),
            ]),
          ]),
      },
      report,
    ),
  ]),
]);
```

The template gets `{ index, pageNumber }`: `index` counts the pages of this Flow from 0, so the first
page can carry the title and the others a running head. A `ColumnBreak` in the content moves on to the
sidebar.

A `Region` is sized by the layout around it, like any element: `Expanded`, a `width` or `height` in
points or `%`, min and max. With nothing given, it fills what it is offered.

| `Flow` option | Default | What it does                                                        |
| ------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `template`    | -       | `({ index, pageNumber }) => element`, built for every page          |
| `gap`         | `0`     | space between the content's elements                                |
| `balance`     | `false` | on the last page, spread the content so the Regions end about equal |

A `SplitView` is exactly this: a `Flow` whose template is a `Row` of `Expanded(Region())`.

### Where a Flow gets its height

A Flow has no height of its own. It takes the rest of the page, or the height of the box it sits in.
On its last page it shrinks to what the content used, so whatever follows sits right below.

In a box with a fixed height, the Flow cannot continue on the next page. What does not fit is cut off
and handled by [`onOverflow`](/docs/pdf/output), like any other block that is too tall.

## What jasy refuses

A mistake in a layout like this would otherwise lose content without a word. Each one throws a named
error that says what to change:

| Error                      | When                                                                       |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `FlowWithoutRegionError`   | the template holds no `Region`, so the content has nowhere to go           |
| `RegionOutsideFlowError`   | a `Region` in the content, or anywhere outside a template                  |
| `RegionReusedError`        | one `Region` on two pages - build the Regions inside the template function |
| `FlowUnboundedError`       | the Flow has no height to take, e.g. in a `Row` without a height           |
| `FlowRegionsEmptyError`    | every `Region` ends up 0 wide or 0 tall                                    |
| `RegionInPageBuilderError` | a `Region` inside a `PageBuilder`, which builds again for every page       |

In Vue, the template is the `#page` slot - see [Components](/docs/vue/components#columns). In React,
it is the `page` render prop - see [Components](/docs/react/components#columns).

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/positioning
Summary: Overlay and crop - badges, ribbons, cut-in titles and watermarks with relative frames and Positioned children.

# Positioning

Most layout flows top to bottom. Sometimes you want one thing to sit ON TOP of the flow: a badge on a
card, a ribbon, a title that cuts into a box, a watermark. `relative` frames and `Positioned` children
do exactly that. The idea is CSS positioning; `Positioned` is the component that does the placing.

## A badge on a card

Mark a `Box` as a frame with `relative: true`. Inside it, wrap anything in `Positioned` and give it
offsets from the frame's edges. A `Positioned` child is OUT OF FLOW: it reserves no space and pushes
nothing, it just draws where you put it. A negative offset pokes it outside the frame, the "cutting in"
look.

```ts
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { Document, Page, Box, Text, Positioned, renderToBytes } from "@jasy/pdf";

const tag = (bg: string, fg: string, t: string) =>
  Box({ bg, radius: 6, padding: { x: 11, y: 6 } }, [Text(t, { size: 11, bold: true, color: fg })]);

async function build() {
  const doc = Document([
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56 }, [
      Box({ relative: true, bg: "#eef3fb", border: "#1450aa", radius: 12, padding: 24 }, [
        Text("Project Aurora", { size: 18, bold: true, color: "#0a2348" }),
        Text("Badges anchor to the card's corners.", { size: 12, color: "gray" }),
        Positioned({ top: -12, left: -12 }, tag("#f3dc29", "#0a2348", "NEW")), // pokes out
        Positioned({ top: 14, right: 14 }, tag("#1450aa", "#ffffff", "v2")), // inside the corner
      ]),
    ]),
  ]);

  writeFileSync("badge.pdf", await renderToBytes(doc));
}

build();
```

## Anchoring

There are two ways to place a child - use whichever reads best, even one per axis.

**Pin to an edge.** `top` / `left` / `right` / `bottom` are distances from the frame's edges. Set one
per axis; the child shrink-wraps to its content, and a negative value pokes it out.

```ts
Positioned({ top: 14, right: 14 }, badge); // inside the top-right corner
Positioned({ bottom: -10, left: -10 }, badge); // pokes out the bottom-left
```

Set **both** edges of an axis and the child spans between them: `left` and `right` give it the width in
between, `top` and `bottom` the height.

`Positioned` only places; the child keeps its own size. With one edge, a long text stays on one line
and runs past the frame. To make it wrap, give it a width - span it, or size the child:

```ts
Positioned({ top: 0, left: 20, right: 20 }, Text(note)); // wraps between the two edges
Positioned({ top: 0, left: 20 }, Box({ width: 160 }, [Text(note)])); // wraps at 160
```

**Anchor it.** `h` and `v` snap the child to a point - `start`, `center` or `end` on each axis - and
`x` / `y` nudge it from there. So "dead center, ten points up" is `{ h: "center", v: "center", y: -10 }`.
This is the thing edges cannot do cleanly: center.

```ts
Positioned({ h: "center", v: "center" }, watermark); // dead center of the frame
Positioned({ h: "end", v: "end", x: -8, y: -8 }, stamp); // bottom-right, inset 8
Positioned({ h: "center", v: "start", y: 12 }, ribbon); // top-center, nudged 12 down
```

An edge wins over an anchor on the same axis. With no `relative` ancestor, a `Positioned` anchors to
the page's content box.

## Stacking with zIndex (since beta.5)

Without a `zIndex`, what is written later paints on top - a `Positioned` written before the text sits
under it, one written after sits over it. `zIndex` sets the order instead: higher paints over lower, a
positive one over the frame's other content, a negative one under it (but over the frame's own
background). Equal values keep the written order; `0` is the same as none.

```ts
Box({ relative: true, height: 130 }, [
  Positioned({ top: 30, left: 60, zIndex: 2 }, blueCard),
  Positioned({ top: 50, left: 120, zIndex: 3 }, yellowCard), // on top
  Positioned({ top: 10, left: 0, zIndex: 1 }, navyCard), // at the bottom, though written last
]);
```

The order holds across the whole frame: a `Positioned` inside another one is sorted with all the
others, so a badge deep in one card can sit above a card written after it. Two places keep their own
order: a Box with `overflow: "hidden"` and a `Rotated`. A `Positioned` inside one of them is sorted
there and never leaves the clip or the turn it was written in.

## Cropping with overflow

A frame's `overflow` decides what happens to a child that runs past its edge: `"visible"` (the default)
lets it spill, `"hidden"` crops it at the frame, rounded corners and all. Here is the **same card**
twice, side by side, with only `overflow` changed.

```ts
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { Document, Page, Row, Box, Text, Positioned, Expanded, renderToBytes } from "@jasy/pdf";

// a blue box pinned inside the card, extending past its bottom edge
const card = (overflow: "visible" | "hidden") =>
  Box(
    {
      relative: true,
      overflow,
      bg: "#eef3fb",
      border: "#1450aa",
      radius: 10,
      height: 70,
      padding: 14,
    },
    [
      Text(`overflow: "${overflow}"`, { size: 12, bold: true, color: "#0a2348" }),
      Positioned(
        { top: 34, left: 14 },
        Box({ bg: "#1450aa", radius: 8, width: 170, height: 100, padding: 12 }, [
          Text("Pinned inside the card, it extends past the bottom edge.", {
            size: 10,
            color: "#ffffff",
          }),
        ]),
      ),
    ],
  );

async function build() {
  const doc = Document([
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56 }, [
      Row({ gap: 24 }, [Expanded(card("visible")), Expanded(card("hidden"))]),
    ]),
  ]);

  writeFileSync("overflow.pdf", await renderToBytes(doc));
}

build();
```

Left, the blue box hangs past the card. Right, the identical box is cropped flush at the card's edge.
`overflow: "hidden"` also crops an `Image` to a rounded box, a clean way to get a rounded or circular
photo.

## A reusable component

A component is just a function returning a tree, so "a card with a cut-in title" is a few lines you
reuse everywhere.

```ts
import { Box, Padding, Positioned, Text, type PDFElement } from "@jasy/pdf";

const TitledCard = (title: string, body: PDFElement) =>
  Box({ relative: true, overflow: "hidden", bg: "#eef3fb", radius: 10 }, [
    Padding(20, body),
    Positioned(
      { top: -10, left: -10 },
      Box({ bg: "#1450aa", radius: 6, padding: { x: 12, y: 6 } }, [
        Text(title, { color: "white", bold: true }),
      ]),
    ),
  ]);
```

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/encryption
Summary: Lock a PDF with a password. AES-256, the newest standard, in pure JavaScript - the same code in Node and the browser.

# Encryption

Protect a PDF with a password and jasy encrypts it with **AES-256** (V5/R6, the newest handler in the PDF
spec). It runs on the platform's WebCrypto, so there are no native dependencies and no Java - the same code
encrypts in Node and right in the browser.

## Set a password

Pass an `encrypt` option to `renderToBytes` (or `renderPdf`). A `userPassword` is all you need - any viewer
asks for it before it opens the document.

```ts
import { Document, Page, Text, renderToBytes } from "@jasy/pdf";

const doc = Document([Page([Text("Confidential")])]);

const bytes = await renderToBytes(doc, {
  encrypt: { userPassword: "secret" },
});
```

## Owner password and permissions

Add an `ownerPassword` for full rights, and `permissions` to allow or deny actions. The owner password
