defaults to the user password when you leave it out, and every permission defaults to allowed.

```ts
const bytes = await renderToBytes(doc, {
  encrypt: {
    userPassword: "secret", // to open the document
    ownerPassword: "owner", // full rights
    permissions: {
      printing: false, // disallow printing
      copying: false, // disallow text/content extraction
      modifying: true,
      annotating: true,
    },
  },
});
```

## Opening one

The other half: jasy **reads** encrypted PDFs too, which is what makes filling a protected form
possible. Pass the password and everything downstream stays ordinary:

```ts
import { PdfDocument, fillForm } from "@jasy/pdf/edit";

const doc = await PdfDocument.open(bytes, { password: "secret" });
const { bytes: filled } = await fillForm(bytes, { name: "Ada" }, { password: "secret" });
```

**Reading is broad, writing is narrow.** jasy opens AES-256 (R6, R5), AES-128 (R4) and RC4 (R2/R3),
because those files exist and you may have to open one. It writes **only AES-256 R6**: handing someone
protection that is known to be broken is not a feature, so the legacy handler refuses to encrypt.

Worth knowing when you compare: PDFKit and react-pdf both default to **40-bit RC4** when you ask for a
password, and neither can emit R6 at all. Ghostscript 10 refuses anything past R3.

The errors are named, never generic: no password, wrong password, or a revision jasy does not
implement - three different things a caller can act on differently.

## Good to know

- **AES-256, R6.** The current ISO 32000-2 handler - not the older revisions some libraries still ship.
- **Pure JS, isomorphic.** WebCrypto under the hood: no native crypto, zero extra dependencies, identical in
  Node and the browser.
- **Vue, React and Nuxt too.** In `@jasy/vue` pass it as the third argument -
  `renderToPdf(Doc, props, { encrypt: { userPassword: "secret" } })`. In `@jasy/react` it is the second -
  `renderToPdf(<Doc />, { encrypt: { userPassword: "secret" } })`. In `@jasy/nuxt` use `renderOptions`.
- **Not for PDF/A.** PDF/A (and therefore ZUGFeRD / Factur-X invoices) forbids encryption, so encrypting one
  is rejected with a clear error.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/emoji
Summary: Real color emoji rendered as vectors in pure TypeScript - no headless browser, no CDN required. COLR/CPAL fonts, drawn layer by layer.

# Emoji

jasy renders color emoji as **real vector layers**, in pure TypeScript. It parses the color-font tables
(COLR / CPAL) itself and draws every layer - solid fills and gradients alike - straight into the PDF. No
headless browser, no CDN round-trip, no bitmap fallback. `@react-pdf/renderer`, by contrast, only fetches
Twemoji PNGs from a CDN; jasy owns the whole path natively.

## Just write the emoji

Point the document at an emoji source with `emoji`, register that font, and emoji in any string render in
color - even inside your normal text font.

```ts
import { writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { Document, Page, Text, renderToBytes } from "@jasy/pdf";

async function build() {
  const doc = Document({ emoji: "NotoColorEmoji" }, [
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 56 }, [Text("Ready to ship 🚀🎉", { size: 24 })]),
  ]);

  doc.addFont("NotoColorEmoji", "NotoColorEmoji.ttf"); // a COLR/CPAL color font

  writeFileSync("emoji.pdf", await renderToBytes(doc));
}

build();
```

The text itself stays in your regular font; only the code points that font can't color-render come from
the emoji source. Spacing stays correct either way, because measuring and drawing share the same source.

## From a CDN instead of a font

Prefer the react-pdf style? Give `emoji` a `url` and jasy fetches one image per emoji from it
(`${url}${codePointHex}.${format}`) and embeds it, transparency included. Handy when you don't want to
ship a font, though the font source is smaller, offline and sharper.

```ts
const doc = Document(
  {
    emoji: {
      url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/jdecked/twemoji@latest/assets/72x72/",
      format: "png",
    },
  },
  [Page([Text("Shipping with Twemoji 😄")])],
);
```

## Good to know

- **Real vectors, pure TS.** COLR/CPAL v0 (flat layers) and v1 (gradients and transforms) are parsed and
  drawn as PDF paths and shadings - the full Noto Color Emoji set renders. No browser, no JVM.
- **A color font drawn as vectors isn't embedded** as a font program, so it adds no `/FontFile` weight.
- **Single code points today.** One-code-point emoji (~95% of everyday use) are covered; multi-code-point
  sequences (flags, ZWJ combos, skin-tone modifiers) are deferred.
- **Bitmap color fonts** (Apple Color Emoji's `sbix`, the CBDT Noto build) and CFF-outline color fonts are
  not parsed yet - use a `glyf`-outline COLR font like Noto Color Emoji or Twemoji, or the CDN source.
- **Vue, React and Nuxt too.** Pass `emoji` on the document options exactly as above.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/accessibility
Summary: Emit a tagged, PDF/UA-1 accessible PDF that screen readers can navigate - it passes veraPDF's machine checks. One flag, plus a role here and there.

# Accessibility

jasy can emit a **tagged PDF** with a full structure tree, so screen readers can read the document in
order, announce headings, and describe images. The output is **PDF/UA-1** and passes **veraPDF**'s
compliance check. `@react-pdf/renderer` produces untagged PDFs, so this is a genuine jasy differentiator.

## Turn it on

Pass `accessible` to `renderToBytes` (or `renderPdf`). Add a `lang` and a `title` - both are part of the
standard, and a title is required for full conformance.

```ts
import { Document, Page, Text, renderToBytes } from "@jasy/pdf";

const doc = Document([
  Page([
    Text("Quarterly Report", { role: "h1", size: 24, bold: true }),
    Text("Revenue grew across every region this quarter."),
  ]),
]);

const bytes = await renderToBytes(doc, {
  accessible: true,
  lang: "en-US",
  title: "Quarterly Report",
});
```

## Declare what things are

The engine builds the structure tree; your components only declare their role.

- **Headings and paragraphs** - `Text({ role })`, where `role` is `"h1"` through `"h6"` or `"p"`.
- **Images** - `Image({ alt })` gives the figure its alternate text.
- **Tables** - a `Table` is tagged automatically (table, rows, header and data cells), no extra work.
- **Decoration** - anything without a role is marked as an artifact, so screen readers skip it.

```ts
Text("Section title", { role: "h2" });
Image("chart.png", { alt: "Revenue by region, Q3" });
```

## Good to know

- **Verified, not claimed.** The output is checked with veraPDF against PDF/UA-1; a split paragraph or a
  table that flows across pages stays one logical element in the tree.
- **Full conformance needs embedded fonts and a title** - the same rule as PDF/A. Use a custom TrueType
  font (see [Fonts](/docs/pdf/fonts)) and pass a `title`.
- **Off by default, zero cost.** Without `accessible` the bytes are identical to before - tagging adds
  nothing until you ask for it.
- **Vue, React and Nuxt too.** Pass the same options through `renderToPdf` / `renderOptions`.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/rotate
Summary: Rotate anything - a diagonal PAID stamp, a watermark, a vertical table label. Rotated for any angle, RotatedBox for layout-aware quarter-turns.

# Rotate

Two tools, for two different jobs: **`Rotated`** spins a subtree at any angle for stamps and
watermarks, and **`RotatedBox`** does layout-aware quarter-turns for vertical labels. Both rotate
around the element's center.

## Rotated - a stamp or watermark

`Rotated({ angle }, child)` rotates `child` by `angle` degrees (clockwise) around its center, exactly
like CSS `transform: rotate()`. It is **paint-only**: the child keeps its normal layout box, so the
spun drawing can overflow its slot and siblings never reflow around it. In a `Row` or `Column` the
child is the item (changed in beta.5) - an `Expanded` inside a `Rotated` still flexes. That is what you want for a
stamp - it should not push the content underneath around.

Pair it with a `relative` Box and `Positioned` to lay a "BEZAHLT" / "PAID" stamp diagonally across a
document:

```ts
import { Box, Text, Positioned, Rotated } from "@jasy/pdf";

Box({ relative: true }, [
  // ... your invoice ...
  Positioned(
    { h: "center", v: "center" },
    Rotated(
      { angle: -18 },
      Box({ border: "#c0392b", borderWidth: 4, radius: 12, padding: { x: 26, y: 12 } }, [
        Text("BEZAHLT", { size: 40, bold: true, color: "#c0392b" }),
      ]),
    ),
  ),
]);
```

`Positioned({ h: "center", v: "center" })` centers the stamp on the card; `Rotated` tilts it in place
around its own center. See the **Stamped invoice** in the [showroom](/showroom).

## RotatedBox - a vertical label

A stamp does not change layout - but a vertical label beside a table should. `RotatedBox({ turns }, child)`
does whole quarter-turns and is **layout-aware**: a 90 or 270 turn swaps the box's width and height, so it
reserves its narrow width and tall height, and siblings lay out around it. `turns` is the number of
clockwise quarter-turns (`1` = 90 deg, `2` = 180, `3` = 270).

```ts
import { Row, Column, Text, RotatedBox } from "@jasy/pdf";

Row({ align: "center" }, [
  RotatedBox({ turns: 3 }, Text("SECTION A", { size: 16, bold: true })), // reads bottom-to-top
  Column({ gap: 6 }, rows), // the list; the label sits tight to its left, vertically centered
]);
```

Because the rotated box reports its real footprint, the label takes only its narrow width (no dead
space) and stays vertically centered against the list.

## Which one

- **`Rotated`** - any angle, layout untouched. Stamps, watermarks, decorative badges.
- **`RotatedBox`** - 90 deg steps, layout follows. Vertical table / column labels.

## Good to know

- **Pivot is the center.** Both rotate around the element's box center (CSS `transform-origin: center`).
- **Rotate is paint-only in `Rotated`.** After a 90 deg `Rotated`, the layout box does NOT become tall -
  it stays as it was and the drawing overflows. Reach for `RotatedBox` when you want the layout to follow.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/navigation
Summary: Links to the web, jumps inside the document, and a bookmark tree in the viewer's sidebar. Link, Anchor and Bookmark.

# Navigation

Three tools, for three different jobs. **`Link`** makes something clickable, either to the web or to
another place in the same document. **`Anchor`** marks that place. **`Bookmark`** fills the outline tree
your PDF viewer shows in its sidebar.

## Links to the web

Wrap any element and its whole box becomes the hit area - an image, a box, a row.

```ts
Link({ href: "https://jasy.dev" }, Box({ bg: "#f3dc29", padding: 12 }, [Text("Read the docs")]));
```

A link draws nothing of its own, so style the child if you want it to look like one.

For a link on part of a line, put `href` on a `span` instead. Only that run becomes clickable, and the
text keeps flowing around it:

```ts
Paragraph([
  span("Built with "),
  span("jasy", { href: "https://jasy.dev", color: "#1450aa", bold: true }),
  span(", and the rest of this sentence is not a link."),
]);
```

A span that wraps onto a second line gets a clickable rectangle per line, so the whole run stays
clickable. A plain string works too: `Text("jasy.dev", { href: "https://jasy.dev" })` links the entire
text.

## Jumps inside the document

Mark a target with `Anchor`, then point a link at it with `to` instead of `href`. This is how you build a
table of contents that actually works.

```ts
import { Document, Page, Column, Row, Text, Link, Anchor } from "@jasy/pdf";

const doc = Document([
  Page([
    Column([
      Text("Contents", { size: 22, bold: true }),
      Link({ to: "install" }, Row({ justify: "between" }, [Text("1. Installation"), Text("jump")])),
    ]),
  ]),
  Page([Anchor({ name: "install" }, Text("1. Installation", { size: 22, bold: true }))]),
]);
```

`to` also works on a `span`, for a "back to the top" in the middle of a sentence. A `Link` takes exactly
one of `href` or `to`; giving it both, or neither, throws.

> The anchor may live on a page that has not been rendered yet - jasy resolves it by name at the end, so
> forward references are not a problem you have to think about.

> Careful with the word: `Anchor` here is a jump target. That is unrelated to the `h` / `v` anchoring of a
> [`Positioned`](/docs/pdf/positioning) child, which is about placement.

## Bookmarks

`Bookmark` adds an entry to the outline tree - the panel your viewer opens next to the page. `level`
nests it, so chapters and their sections form a collapsible tree.

```ts
Bookmark({ title: "2. Installation", level: 1 }, Text("2. Installation", { size: 22, bold: true }));
Bookmark(
  { title: "2.1 Requirements", level: 2 },
  Text("2.1 Requirements", { size: 16, bold: true }),
);
```

A `level: 2` bookmark hangs under the nearest preceding `level: 1`. Bookmarks are layout-transparent:
the child renders exactly as it would on its own.

## One heading, both jobs

A chapter heading usually wants to be a sidebar entry _and_ a jump target. Nest them, and it is both:

```ts
Bookmark(
  { title: "2. Installation", level: 1 },
  Anchor({ name: "install" }, Text("2. Installation", { size: 22, bold: true })),
);
```

See the [Handbook](/showroom) in the showroom for all of it in one document: a clickable contents page,
a bookmark tree, and links back to the top.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/drawing
Summary: Place an SVG logo as a real vector, or draw a chart yourself with a typed pen - both writing into the same vector layer.

# SVG and Canvas

PDF is a vector format. A logo pasted in as a PNG throws that away: it goes soft when someone zooms,
fat when someone prints, and it carries pixels into a document that is meant to be archived. jasy
draws vectors instead - either from an SVG file you already have, or from a pen you drive yourself.

## An SVG logo

`Image` recognizes an SVG source by itself, so a logo needs no special handling:

```ts
import { Document, Page, Image, Svg, renderToBytes } from "@jasy/pdf";

Image("logo.svg", { width: 120 }); // a path (Node), bytes, or markup
Svg(markup, { width: 120, alt: "Acme" }); // the same thing, named explicitly
```

With no size it draws at its intrinsic size (changed in beta.5) - the `width`/`height` on the
file, else its `viewBox`, else 300 x 150 px, as in a browser. A user unit is a CSS pixel, 1/96 inch -
the same rule as for a [raster image](/docs/pdf/images) - and `pt`, `pc`, `in`, `cm`, `mm` and `q` are
converted, so `width="100mm"` is 100 mm. If the file gives one side, the other follows the `viewBox`
ratio; a `%` size counts as not given. Before beta.5 a user unit was a point and units were ignored.

Pin one axis and the other follows the ratio, exactly as an unsized `<img>` behaves; wider than the
space it is offered, it is scaled down, never up. The drawing is scaled uniformly and centered inside
its box, which is SVG's own `preserveAspectRatio` default.

The file is read and parsed **when you name it**, not at render time, so a broken path or a malformed
file fails on that line rather than three call frames deep in a render.

### What it draws

| Resolved                                                                                                    | Reported by name, never skipped       |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `path` (arcs, shorthands, relative coordinates), `rect`, `circle`, `ellipse`, `line`, `polyline`, `polygon` | `<text>` - convert it to outlines     |
| `g`, `defs`, `viewBox`, every `transform` function                                                          | `<use>`, `<symbol>`                   |
| presentation attributes, `style=""`, and `<style>` blocks with flat selectors                               | a CSS combinator or pseudo-class      |
| `fill`, `stroke` (width, cap, join, dash), `fill-rule`, opacity                                             | `filter`, `<mask>` - pixel operations |
| `<clipPath>`, `<linearGradient>`, `<radialGradient>`, `href` chains                                         | a gradient on a stroke                |

**SVG is a document format, not a graphics format.** It carries CSS, text layout, filters and
animation, and filters and masks are pixel operations that no vector backend can express - which is
why anything that renders SVG _completely_ owns a rasterizer, and why every PDF library ships a
subset. Ours is above.

The difference is what happens at its edge: an element jasy cannot draw is a **named error with a
fix**, never a silent skip. A dropped element leaves a logo that renders and is quietly wrong, and
nobody finds out. (Measured: react-pdf's `<style>` handling loses every fill of an Illustrator export
made with its default "Internal CSS" option.)

```
@jasy/pdf: the SVG element <text> is not supported yet.
           Convert the text to outlines in your editor - a PDF cannot lay out SVG text.
```

The subset was checked against **10,819 real SVG files** taken off a working machine: 96.4% render.
Correctness is checked against headless Chrome, not against our own reasoning - that is how we found
that the root `<svg>` clips to itself, and that its own `fill="none"` (the Figma export default, in
778 of those files) has to be read or every unfilled shape comes out black.

## Drawing it yourself

`Canvas` is the escape hatch for what no component covers: a sparkline, a seal, a chart, a signature
flourish. You get a box in the layout and a typed pen.

```ts
import { Canvas } from "@jasy/pdf";

Canvas({ height: 46 }, (c, { width, height }) => {
  c.move(0, height).line(20, 12).line(60, 22).line(width, 4);
  c.stroke("#1450aa", { width: 1.5, cap: "round", join: "round" });

  c.circle(width - 4, 4, 2.5).fill("#1450aa");
});
```

The callback is handed the size the layout resolved, so a drawing written against `size.width` works
at any width - put the same function in a 300pt box and a 160pt one and it fits both.

### The pen

| Building a path                                                 | Painting it                                                          |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `move` `line` `curve` `quad` `close`                            | `fill(paint?, { rule })`                                             |
| `rect` `circle` `ellipse` `polygon`                             | `stroke(color?, { width, cap, join, miterLimit, dash, dashOffset })` |
| `path(d)` - SVG path data, through the same reader `Svg()` uses | `fillAndStroke(fill, stroke, opts)`                                  |

Painting finishes the path and starts a new one, so a shape can never leak into the next. `fill` takes
any color form the rest of the API takes - and a gradient, resolved against the shape's own bounding
box, the way `objectBoundingBox` works in SVG.

### Scopes instead of save/restore

A transform or a clip is a **scope that closes itself**. There is no `save()`/`restore()` pair to
forget, and no `lineWidth(2)` that a later `stroke()` happens to pick up:

```ts
Canvas({ width: 90, height: 90 }, (c, { width }) => {
  for (let i = 0; i < 12; i++) {
    c.group({ translate: [width / 2, width / 2], rotate: i * 30 }, (g) => {
      g.rect(-1, -width / 2 + 6, 2, i % 3 === 0 ? 10 : 5).fill("#0a2348");
    });
  }

  c.clipped(
    (clip) => clip.circle(width / 2, width / 2, 20),
    (draw) => draw.rect(0, 0, width, width).fill("#f3dc29"),
  );
});
```

Coordinates are top-left and in points - the same system as every other element and the same as SVG.
`0,0` is the canvas box's own corner.

### It is a block in the layout, not a way around it

A canvas is clipped to its own box, paginates as one unbreakable unit, and can carry `alt` to become a
`Figure` in a tagged PDF. What it deliberately does **not** have is text layout: labels belong in
`Text`, in the tree, where they stay selectable, searchable and tagged.

```ts
Row({ gap: 8, align: "stretch" }, [
  Column(
    { justify: "between", width: 26 },
    ticks.map((t) => Text(String(t), { size: 7 })),
  ),
  Expanded(
    { flex: 1 },
    Column({ gap: 4 }, [
      Canvas({ height: 170, alt: "Monthly revenue" }, barChart),
      Row(
        { justify: "between" },
        months.map((m) => Text(m, { size: 7 })),
      ),
    ]),
  ),
]);
```

That is a real chart: the drawing is a canvas, the axes are text in the layout.

Both are components in Vue, React and Nuxt as well - see the [Vue](/docs/vue/components) and
[React](/docs/react/components) components.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/forms
Summary: Create fillable AcroForm fields, and read, fill and flatten a form that someone else made - all in pure TypeScript.

# Forms

jasy does both halves of the PDF form story: it **creates** fillable fields as ordinary layout
elements, and it **reads and fills** a form that came from somewhere else - a government PDF, a
supplier's order sheet - without touching the rest of the file.

## Creating fields

A field is a layout element like any other. It reserves a box and emits a widget annotation, so it
sits in a `Column`, paginates, and takes the same sizing props as a `Box`.

```ts
import {
  Document,
  Page,
  Column,
  Row,
  Text,
  TextField,
  Checkbox,
  RadioGroup,
  Dropdown,
  ListBox,
  PushButton,
  SignatureField,
  renderToBytes,
} from "@jasy/pdf";

Document([
  Page({ size: "A4", margin: 48, gap: 12 }, [
    Text("Registration", { size: 20, bold: true }),

    TextField({ name: "fullName", width: 260, height: 22 }),
    TextField({ name: "notes", width: 260, height: 60, multiline: true, maxLength: 500 }),

    Checkbox({ name: "agree", label: "I agree to the terms" }),
    RadioGroup({ name: "plan", gap: 8 }, [
      { value: "basic", label: "Basic" },
      { value: "pro", label: "Pro" },
    ]),
    Dropdown({ name: "country", width: 120, height: 22 }, ["DE", "AT", "CH"]),
    ListBox({ name: "topics", width: 160, height: 48 }, ["invoices", "reports"]),

    PushButton({ name: "reset", label: "Reset", action: "reset", width: 80, height: 24 }),
    SignatureField({ name: "signature", width: 200, height: 48 }),
  ]),
]);
```

Seven kinds: `TextField`, `Checkbox`, `Radio` / `RadioGroup`, `Dropdown` (alias `Select`), `ListBox`,
`PushButton` and `SignatureField`. The ones that offer a choice take it as the second argument, the
way `Column` takes its children - a radio choice as `{ value, label }`, a dropdown or list entry as a
plain string.

A `PushButton` does one of three things: `action: "reset"` clears the form, `{ open: url }` follows a
link, `{ submit: url }` posts the values - the last one Acrobat only, since neither poppler nor pdf.js
implements `/SubmitForm`.

### The props every field takes

| Prop                                  | What it does                                                   |
| ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`                                | the key the value is stored under, and the one `fillForm` uses |
| `width`, `height`                     | the box it reserves, in points                                 |
| `tooltip`                             | hover text (`/TU`), and what a screen reader announces         |
| `readOnly`                            | shown but not editable                                         |
| `required`                            | must be filled before the form is submitted                    |
| `hidden`                              | not shown at all, on screen or in print                        |
| `print`                               | `false` keeps it on screen only                                |
| `border`, `background`, `borderWidth` | its appearance; a field draws **no border by default**         |
| `color`, `fontSize`                   | how the value is drawn inside the box                          |

A field with no `border` is invisible until it is clicked, exactly like a browser input with
`border: none`. That is a reasonable default when you draw your own boxes underneath, and a surprise
otherwise - so give it one:

```ts
TextField({ name: "fullName", width: 260, height: 22, border: "#aab3c2", background: "#fbfcfe" });
```

### And the ones only some of them take

| Field           | Prop                                  | What it does                                       |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `TextField`     | `value`                               | the value it starts with                           |
|                 | `multiline`                           | accept several lines - give it a matching `height` |
|                 | `password`                            | mask the characters                                |
|                 | `maxLength`                           | refuse anything longer, on entry and on fill       |
|                 | `align`                               | `"left"` \| `"center"` \| `"right"`                |
| `Checkbox`      | `checked`                             | starts ticked                                      |
|                 | `onValue`                             | what is stored when ticked (default `"Yes"`)       |
|                 | `size`                                | box side length in points                          |
| `RadioGroup`    | `value`                               | which option starts selected, by its value         |
|                 | `size`, `gap`                         | button diameter, and the space between buttons     |
| `Dropdown`      | `value`, `editable`                   | the starting choice; `editable` allows free text   |
| `ListBox`       | `value`, `multiSelect`                | the starting choice; several selectable at once    |
| `PushButton`    | `action`                              | `"reset"` \| `{ open: url }` \| `{ submit: url }`  |
| labelled fields | `label`                               | the text drawn beside a checkbox, radio or button  |
|                 | `labelSize`, `labelColor`, `labelGap` | how that label is set and how far it sits away     |

A `Radio` option also takes `selected` when you build the buttons yourself instead of handing
`RadioGroup` a list.

jasy **bakes an appearance** for every field, so the value is visible before a reader redraws it. Opt
out with `renderToBytes(doc, { fieldAppearances: false })` if you would rather the viewer draw
everything. Field text is deliberately unkerned: viewers do not kern field text, and a baked
appearance has to match what the viewer will redraw over it.

## Filling a form somebody else made

The reader lives behind its own entry point, so a project that only ever generates PDFs never bundles
it:

```ts
import { readAcroForm, fillForm, flattenForm, PdfDocument } from "@jasy/pdf/edit";

// What is in there? Each field comes back with its name, type, current value, options and flags.
const form = readAcroForm(await PdfDocument.open(bytes));
form.fields.map((f) => `${f.name} (${f.type})`); // ["fullName (Tx)", "agree (Btn)", ...]
```

Each field it hands back:

| Property          | What it is                                                                    |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`            | the fully qualified name - the `/T` values from the root down, joined by dots |
| `type`            | `"Tx"` text · `"Btn"` button · `"Ch"` choice · `"Sig"` signature              |
| `value`, `values` | what it currently holds; `values` for a multi-select choice                   |
| `options`         | a choice field's entries, as `{ value, label }`                               |
| `onValues`        | every export name a check box or radio can take, besides `Off`                |
| `maxLen`          | `/MaxLen`, inherited down the tree like the type                              |
| `flags`           | the `/Ff` bits, already merged with anything inherited                        |
| `widgets`         | the boxes that display it - a radio group has one per button                  |
| `needsAppearance` | no widget carries a drawn appearance, so filling it has to generate one       |

Note the name: the creation option is `maxLength`, the field read back reports **`maxLen`**, because
that side mirrors the PDF key `/MaxLen` rather than the factory.

```ts
const { bytes: filled, warnings } = await fillForm(bytes, {
  fullName: "Ada Lovelace",
  agree: true,
  country: "DE",
});
```

Both `fillForm` and `flattenForm` return a **result object** - `bytes` plus what was touched
(`filled`, `flattened`) and any `warnings` - rather than raw bytes, so nothing about the operation is
lost on the way back.

You pass **values**, not object mutations. The form is a contract, and every way of breaking it is a
named error rather than a silent no-op: an unknown field name, a value of the wrong type for the kind,
a string past the field's `MaxLen`, a choice that is not in the list, a read-only field, a signature
field, a push button.

### Flattening

`flattenForm` stamps each field's appearance onto the page and removes the widget, so the values can
no longer be edited. `fillForm(bytes, values, { flatten: true })` does both in one pass:

```ts
const { bytes: frozen } = await fillForm(bytes, { fullName: "Ada" }, { flatten: true });

// or on its own, optionally for named fields only
const { bytes: partly } = await flattenForm(filled, { fields: ["fullName"] });
```

### The original file stays a prefix

Saving is an **incremental update**: the original bytes are kept verbatim, the changed objects are
appended, and the new cross-reference table chains back with `/Prev`. That gives a property you can
check with a diff - **the file you passed in is a literal prefix of the file you get back**. Nothing
was rewritten behind your back, and any signature over the original bytes still covers them.

An encrypted PDF works too: `fillForm(bytes, values, { password })` decrypts, fills and re-encrypts,
including the strings it carries over.

### Errors you can catch, not strings you have to match

Every refusal has a type, so a caller can tell one apart from another without reading messages:

```ts
import {
  fillForm,
  FillError,
  FlattenError,
  PdfEncryptedError,
  PdfStreamTooLargeError,
} from "@jasy/pdf/edit";

try {
  await fillForm(bytes, { nope: "x" });
} catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof FillError) {
    // 'no such field: "nope". This form has: "fullName", "agree"'
  }
}
```

`PdfEncryptedError` says which of the three things went wrong - no password, wrong password, or a
revision jasy does not implement. `PdfStreamTooLargeError` is the zip-bomb guard: a compressed stream
that would inflate past **64 MB** is refused rather than decompressed into memory. Raise or lower it
per call with `maxStreamSize`, and read the default from `DEFAULT_MAX_STREAM_SIZE`:

```ts
await fillForm(bytes, values, { maxStreamSize: 8 * 1024 * 1024 });
```

The guard is not free advice: the obvious implementation is wrong, because `fflate` does not throw on
an over-long inflate - it **truncates silently**, which would trade a crash for quiet data corruption.
jasy streams the input and checks the total as it grows.

### Reading is broad, writing is narrow

jasy **opens** AES-256 (R6, R5), AES-128 (R4) and RC4 (R2/R3), because those files exist and you may
have to fill one. It **writes** only AES-256 R6 - the newest standard. Handing someone protection that
is known to be broken is not a feature, so the legacy handler refuses to encrypt.

Worth knowing when you compare: PDFKit and react-pdf both default to **40-bit RC4** when you ask them
for a password, and neither can emit R6 at all.

## The bug this design came from

A filled field showed nothing until you clicked it. The obvious story - "the viewer redraws lazily" -
was wrong, and a second implementation proved it: react-pdf's filled file behaved fine. The difference
was that theirs carried **no** appearance, so the viewer had to draw, while ours carried a **stale**
one from creation. We had written a new value and left the old picture behind: a self-contradicting
document.

So on fill, a text or choice field's appearance is **dropped**; a button's is kept, because its
appearance holds its on and off states and only the selector moves.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/pdf/output
Summary: Everything renderToBytes accepts - embedded fonts, file attachments, PDF/A metadata, compression, kerning and the callbacks that tell you what happened.

# Output options

`renderToBytes(doc, options)` turns a document into bytes. Everything on this page is optional -
`renderToBytes(doc)` on its own already produces a valid PDF.

```ts
import { renderToBytes } from "@jasy/pdf";

const bytes = await renderToBytes(doc, {
  title: "Q3 report",
  accessible: true,
});
```

## Files inside the PDF

A PDF can carry other files. That is how a ZUGFeRD invoice hides its XML inside the page a human
reads, and you can use it for anything else: the CSV a table was built from, the contract a quote
refers to, the source of a chart.

```ts
const bytes = await renderToBytes(doc, {
  attachments: [
    {
      name: "figures.csv",
      data: new TextEncoder().encode("month,revenue\n2026-06,42000\n"),
      mimeType: "text/csv",
      relationship: "Source",
      description: "The numbers behind the chart on page 2",
    },
  ],
});
```

| Field          | Meaning                                                                  |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `name`         | the file name a reader shows, e.g. `"figures.csv"`                       |
| `data`         | the bytes (`Uint8Array`)                                                 |
| `mimeType`     | e.g. `"text/csv"`; default `"application/octet-stream"`                  |
| `relationship` | `/AFRelationship`: `"Data"`, `"Source"`, `"Alternative"`, `"Supplement"` |
| `description`  | free text shown next to the file                                         |

`relationship` says what the file IS to the document rather than how it is stored, and a validator
checks it: ZUGFeRD requires `"Data"` for its `factur-x.xml`, because the XML **is** the invoice, not a
supplement to it. Attachments are written as **associated files**, which is what PDF/A-3 and PDF 2.0
require - a plain `/EmbeddedFiles` entry would not satisfy either.

### Reading them back (since beta.4)

`readAttachments` lists every file a PDF carries - from any producer, not only jasy:

```ts
import { PdfDocument, readAttachments } from "@jasy/pdf/edit";

const doc = await PdfDocument.open(bytes, { password }); // password only if it is encrypted
for (const file of readAttachments(doc)) {
  console.log(file.name, file.mimeType, file.relationship, file.locations);
  const data = file.bytes(); // or file.text() for XML, CSV, ...
}
```

It finds a file wherever a PDF may keep one - the document's attachment list, the PDF/A-3 associated
files, and file annotations on a page - and `locations` says where each one hangs. One file listed in
two places is one entry; two files with the same name are two, so deciding what to do with a duplicate
name stays your call. `bytes()` hands back exactly what was embedded: decrypted, every standard filter
decoded, and checked against the file's own checksum. Data that does not match it, or a filter that
cannot be decoded, throws an `AttachmentError` instead of returning something close.

## Building a PDF/A yourself

[`@jasy/e-invoice`](/docs/invoicing) does all of this for you, and for an invoice you should let it.
These options exist because the same machinery is useful for any archival PDF - a contract, a report
that has to survive a decade:

```ts
const bytes = await renderToBytes(doc, {
  pdfVersion: "1.7", // PDF/A-3 needs it; default "1.4"
  documentId: true, // a trailer /ID, which PDF/A requires
  outputIntent: sRGBProfileBytes, // an ICC profile, so color is defined
  xmp: xmpPacket, // the XMP that DECLARES the conformance level
  standardFonts: false, // no Helvetica: PDF/A wants every font embedded
  fonts: { Helvetica: myEmbeddedFace },
});
```

Two of those are easy to get wrong:

- **`standardFonts: false` is the point, not a detail.** PDF/A forbids relying on the reader's fonts,
  and the standard 14 are exactly that. Turning them off means every font name you use must arrive
  through `fonts` - which is why `@jasy/e-invoice` ships the Liberation faces under the names
  `Helvetica`, `Times` and `Courier`.
- **`xmp` is what a validator reads.** The conformance level lives in the XMP packet, not in the
  structure. Getting the structure right and the packet wrong produces a file that claims nothing.

`documentId` writes a **deterministic** `/ID`: it is a hash of the objects, not a random number and not
the clock. That is what lets the same document render byte-identically twice, so an archived file stays
re-derivable years later.

## Typography and size

| Option     | Default | What it does                                                            |
| ---------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fonts`    | -       | embedded faces, keyed by the name used in `Text({ font })`              |
| `kerning`  | `true`  | space glyph pairs from the font's own data; `false` is the older output |
| `compress` | `true`  | FlateDecode the streams; `false` gives a greppable, readable PDF        |

`compress: false` is a debugging tool worth knowing about: the content stream becomes plain text, so
you can open the PDF in an editor and read the operators jasy wrote.

## Telling you what happened

```ts
const bytes = await renderToBytes(doc, {
  onOverflow: "warn",
  onMissingGlyphs: (chars) => report(`not drawable: ${chars.join(" ")}`),
  onDiagnostic: (d) => report(`${d.code} in ${d.element} "${d.text}" on page ${d.page}`),
});
```

- **`onOverflow`** - what to do when a single block is taller than a whole page and cannot be broken.
  `"error"` (default) throws, `"warn"` logs, `"ignore"` is silent. It is **clipped either way**: the
  alternative is a pagination loop that never ends.
- **`onMissingGlyphs`** - called once with any characters no font could draw. They are removed rather
  than written as the font's `.notdef` box, which PDF/A forbids. Deliberately a callback and not a
  policy: a missing tick mark must never stop an invoice from being produced, but your application
  should be able to say which character went missing.
- **`onDiagnostic`** (since beta.4) - one channel for everything jasy has to say about a document it rendered anyway.
  Each finding has a stable `code`, the element as you wrote it (`"Box"`, `"Text"`), its first text and
  the page:

  | `code`                                    | Meaning                                                                                 |
  | ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | `page-break-ignored`                      | a `PageBreak` inside a `Row` or a `PageBuilder`, which never paginate                   |
  | `column-break-ignored` (since beta.5) | a `ColumnBreak` outside the [columns](/docs/pdf/columns) of a `Flow`                    |
  | `break-ignored`                           | `breakBefore` / `breakAfter` on something inside a `Row` or a table row                 |
  | `keep-together-split`                     | a `keepTogether` group holds a forced break; the break wins                             |
  | `overflow-clipped`                        | a block taller than a page that cannot break (with `onOverflow` not `"error"`)          |
  | `overflow-wide` (since beta.5)        | a word that cannot break, or a `Row` whose children need more room, drawn past the edge |
  | `missing-glyphs`                          | characters no font could draw, per `Text`                                               |
  | `image-unsized` (since beta.5)        | an image whose own size was unknown at layout - a URL first built in a `PageBuilder`    |

  Without a handler nothing changes: what warned before still goes to the console.

## Metadata and access

| Option       | What it does                                                                   |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `title`      | the document title - used by readers, and required for a conformant tagged PDF |
| `lang`       | document language, e.g. `"de-DE"` (default `"en-US"`)                          |
| `accessible` | emit a tagged structure tree - see [Accessibility](/docs/pdf/accessibility)    |
| `encrypt`    | AES-256 password protection - see [Encryption](/docs/pdf/encryption)           |

`encrypt` and PDF/A are mutually exclusive, and jasy says so rather than producing a file that fails
validation later: PDF/A forbids encryption, so encrypting a ZUGFeRD invoice throws.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/vue
Summary: Author PDFs as Vue components with @jasy/vue and render them right in the browser - or on a server, the same call.

# PDFs in Vue

`@jasy/vue` lets you author a PDF the way you build an app: a tree of components, with props, slots and
your reactive data. It is a thin Vue custom renderer over the [`@jasy/pdf`](/docs/pdf) engine, so you
get its real layout and pagination - and because the engine is isomorphic, `renderToPdf` produces the
PDF bytes **right in the browser**. No headless browser, no server round-trip, no Java.

If you have used `@react-pdf/renderer` on the React side this will feel familiar, with one difference:
the same call also runs entirely client-side. On React yourself? The same components are in
[`@jasy/react`](/docs/react).

## Install

```bash
pnpm add @jasy/vue vue
```

`vue` is a peer dependency, and `@jasy/pdf` comes along automatically. You import everything you need -
the components and the render function - from `@jasy/vue`.

## Import the components

Import the ones you need from `@jasy/vue`. In Vue you are in charge of what is in scope, so a name like
`Text` or `Image` never clashes with another library:

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import { Document, Page, Text } from "@jasy/vue";
</script>
```

> Using it in Nuxt? The [`@jasy/nuxt`](/docs/nuxt) module auto-registers the components (no imports) and
> can prefix them to dodge clashes.

## Your first PDF component

A document component's root is always `<Document>`. Everything else nests inside, exactly like the
engine's element tree.

```vue
<!-- Invoice.vue -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { Document, Page, Row, Box, Text, Divider } from "@jasy/vue";

defineProps<{ customer: string; total: number }>();
</script>

<template>
  <Document :size="11" color="#1f2937">
    <Page :size="'A4'" :margin="48" :gap="16">
      <Text :size="24" bold color="#0a2348">Invoice #2026-001</Text>
      <Text color="#64748b">Billed to: {{ customer }}</Text>
      <Divider color="#e2e8f0" />

      <Row :justify="'between'">
        <Text>Consulting</Text>
        <Text bold>{{ total }} EUR</Text>
      </Row>

      <Box bg="#0a2348" :padding="12" :radius="6">
        <Text color="#f3dc29" bold>Total due: {{ total }} EUR</Text>
      </Box>
    </Page>
  </Document>
</template>
```

## Render it to a PDF

`renderToPdf` takes the component (and optional props) and returns the PDF as a `Uint8Array`. This runs
in the browser as happily as in Node - the same line of code.

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import { renderToPdf } from "@jasy/vue";
import Invoice from "./Invoice.vue";

async function download() {
  const bytes = await renderToPdf(Invoice, { customer: "ACME GmbH", total: 1190 });
  const url = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([bytes], { type: "application/pdf" }));
  window.open(url);
}
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="download">Download invoice</button>
</template>
```

Need the raw PDF string instead of bytes? Use `renderToPdfString`. On a server, write the bytes to a
file or stream them as a response - it is the same `renderToPdf`.

## Where to next

- [**Components**](/docs/vue/components) - the full set, their props and the `<Page>` header / footer slots.
- [**Data & assets**](/docs/vue/data-and-assets) - reactive data, custom fonts and images.
- [**Creating PDFs**](/docs/pdf) - the underlying engine, its layout primitives and pagination.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/vue/components
Summary: The @jasy/vue component set, their typed props, and the page header / footer slots.

# Components

Every component maps to one engine element, and every option of the engine is a typed prop -
`<Text :size :color bold>` autocompletes and type-checks, and a wrong value (say a
`fit` that does not exist) goes red in your editor. A test holds the props to the engine, so an option
cannot ship in the core without arriving here. Boolean props have a shorthand: `<Text bold>` is
`<Text :bold="true">`.

The full set:

`Document` · `Page` · `Column` · `Row` · `Box` · `Padding` · `Expanded` · `Spacer` · `Divider` ·
`Image` · `Svg` · `Canvas` · `Text` · `Paragraph` · `Span` · `Table` / `TableRow` / `TableCell` ·
`Positioned` · `DefaultTextStyle` · `Link` · `Anchor` · `Bookmark` · `Rotated` · `RotatedBox` ·
`PageBreak` · `KeepTogether` · `PageNumber` · `PageCount` · `SubPageNumber` · `SubPageCount` ·
`PageBuilder` · `SplitView` · `Flow` · `Region` · `ColumnBreak` · `TextField` · `Checkbox` ·
`RadioGroup` · `Dropdown` · `ListBox` · `PushButton` · `SignatureField`.

That is 43 components, and the Nuxt module auto-imports exactly the same 43.

## Structure

### Document

The root of every PDF component. Its text props (`font`, `size`, `color`, `lineHeight`, `align`, `bold`,
`italic`) set the document-wide defaults that everything inside inherits.

| Prop                                      | Type                                                         |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `size`, `color`, `font`, `bold`, `italic` | default text style                                           |
| `align`, `lineHeight`                     | default paragraph style                                      |
| `meta`                                    | `{ title?, author? }`                                        |
| `fonts`                                   | custom fonts, see [Data & assets](/docs/vue/data-and-assets) |

### Page

One physical page. Lays its children out as a column, so `gap`, `justify` and `align` work here too.

| Prop          | Type                                                            |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `size`        | `"A4"`, `"Letter"`, ... or a custom size                        |
| `orientation` | `"portrait"` \| `"landscape"`                                   |
| `margin`      | a number, or per-side insets                                    |
| `gap`         | space between children                                          |
| `justify`     | `"start"` \| `"center"` \| `"end"` \| `"between"` \| `"around"` |
| `align`       | `"start"` \| `"center"` \| `"end"` \| `"stretch"`               |

`<Page>` also takes `#header` and `#footer` slots. They are drawn on every physical page the content
flows onto, and rebuilt per page - which is how `<PageNumber>` knows where it is:

```vue
<template>
  <Document>
    <Page :size="'A4'" :margin="48">
      <template #header>
        <Text :size="9" color="#94a3b8">ACME GmbH - Invoice</Text>
      </template>

      <Text>... long content that paginates across pages ...</Text>

      <template #footer>
        <Row :justify="'between'">
          <Text :size="9" color="#94a3b8">acme.example</Text>
          <Text :size="9" color="#94a3b8">Page footer</Text>
        </Row>
      </template>
    </Page>
  </Document>
</template>
```

## Layout

### Column and Row

Stack children vertically (`Column`) or horizontally (`Row`). Both take the options of the engine's
stacks: `gap`, `justify`, `align`, `wrap`, `reverse`, `align-content`, a `width` and `height` in points
or `"%"`, and the page-break props below.

```vue
<template>
  <Row :gap="12" :justify="'between'" :align="'center'">
    <Text bold>Item</Text>
    <Text>Value</Text>
  </Row>
</template>
```

Every child can leave its line's alignment with `align-self`, move with `order` and take `min-width`,
`max-width`, `min-height`, `max-height` and `aspect-ratio` - see [Layout](/docs/pdf/layout).

### Box

A sized, decorated container: background, border, padding, rounded corners.

| Prop                                                                       | Type                                 |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `bg`                                                                       | a color, or a gradient               |
| `border`                                                                   | a color                              |
| `borderTop` / `borderRight` / `borderBottom` / `borderLeft`, `borderWidth` | per-side border control              |
| `padding`                                                                  | a number, or per-side insets         |
| `width`, `height`                                                          | points, or a percentage like `"50%"` |
| `radius`                                                                   | a number, or per-corner radii        |
| `relative`                                                                 | make it a positioning frame          |
| `overflow`                                                                 | `"hidden"` clips children to the box |

### Padding, Spacer, Expanded, Divider

- `<Padding :insets="16">` - wraps a child in space (a number or per-side insets).
- `<Spacer :flex="1">` - flexible empty space that pushes siblings apart.
- `<Expanded :flex="1">` - a flex child that fills the remaining main-axis space.
- `<Divider color="#e2e8f0" :thickness="1" />` - a rule line.

## Text

### Text, Paragraph and Span

`Text` and `Paragraph` render text; `Span` styles a run inside them.

Every text style the engine has is a prop here - the set is held to the engine by a test, so a style
cannot ship in the core without arriving in Vue.

| Prop                                    | Type                                                         |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `size`, `font`, `color`                 | the basics; `font` also takes a fallback stack               |
| `bold`, `italic`                        | boolean shorthands                                           |
| `align`                                 | `"left"` \| `"center"` \| `"right"` \| `"justify"`           |
| `lineHeight`                            | line spacing multiplier                                      |
| `letterSpacing`, `wordSpacing`          | in points; negative tightens                                 |
| `textIndent`                            | first-line indent, in points                                 |
| `textTransform`                         | `"uppercase"` \| `"lowercase"` \| `"capitalize"` \| `"none"` |
| `underline`, `strikethrough`, `skipInk` | decoration; `skipInk` steps around descenders                |
| `direction`                             | `"ltr"` \| `"rtl"` - Hebrew and Arabic order correctly       |
| `ligatures`                             | `false` turns off `fi`/`fl`/`ffi`, which are on by default   |
| `breakWord`, `hyphenate`                | what to do with a word too long for its box                  |
| `orphans`, `widows`                     | minimum lines kept together at a page break                  |
| `maxLines`, `overflow`                  | `overflow` is `"clip"` \| `"ellipsis"`                       |
| `role`                                  | `"h1"`..`"h6"` \| `"p"` for a tagged, accessible PDF         |
| `href`                                  | link this run to an external URL                             |
| `to`                                    | link this run to an `<Anchor>`                               |

`<Span>` takes the run styles (changed in beta.5) - `size`, `font`, `color`, `bold`, `italic`,
the decorations, `letterSpacing`, `wordSpacing`, `textTransform`, `ligatures`, `breakWord`,
`hyphenate` - plus `href` / `to` and `verticalAlign` (`"super"` \| `"sub"`), which shifts one run's
baseline without resizing it. What belongs to the whole paragraph stays on `<Text>`: `align`,
`lineHeight`, `textIndent`, `direction`, `maxLines`, `overflow`, `orphans`, `widows` and `role`.

```vue
<template>
  <Paragraph>
    Plain text, then a <Span bold color="#1450aa">styled run</Span> in the middle.
  </Paragraph>
</template>
```

`bold` and `italic` are left unset by default, so a `<Text>` inside a bold `<DefaultTextStyle>` stays
bold unless you override it. `<DefaultTextStyle>` re-defaults the text style for a whole subtree, the
per-section counterpart to the `<Document>` defaults.

Putting `href` (or `to`) on a `<Span>` links just that run and lets the sentence flow around it:

```vue
<template>
  <Paragraph>
    Built with <Span href="https://jasy.dev" bold color="#1450aa">jasy</Span>, and this part is not
    a link.
  </Paragraph>
</template>
```

## Image

```vue
<template>
  <Image
    :src="bytes"
    :width="120"
    :height="120"
    :fit="'cover'"
    :align="'top'"
    :radius="8"
    alt="Logo"
  />
</template>
```

`src` takes image bytes (a `Uint8Array`) or a URL; see [Data & assets](/docs/vue/data-and-assets) for
loading them in the browser. `fit` is `"fill"` (the default), `"contain"`, `"cover"` or `"none"`.
`align` (since beta.5) says where the image sits in its box - `"center"` (the default), `"top"`,
`"bottom left"` and so on. Without a size the image is its own size, scaled down to fit; the props are
those of the [`Image` factory](/docs/pdf/images).

An **SVG source is recognized by itself** and stays a vector - no `fit`, `align` or `radius`, since it
is always drawn contained and centered, which is SVG's own default.

## Svg

```vue
<template>
  <Svg :src="logoMarkup" :width="120" alt="Acme" />
</template>
```

`src` takes SVG markup, the file's bytes, or - on the server - a path. With no size it draws at its
intrinsic size; pin one axis and the other follows the `viewBox`. `alt` makes it a `Figure` in a
tagged PDF. See [SVG and Canvas](/docs/pdf/drawing) for what the subset covers.

## Canvas

For a chart, a sparkline or a seal, `<Canvas>` hands your function a typed pen and the size the layout
resolved. `paint` is an ordinary function prop:

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import type { CanvasPainter } from "@jasy/pdf";

const months = [12, 19, 14, 27, 22, 31];

function sparkline(c: CanvasPainter, { width, height }: { width: number; height: number }) {
  const max = Math.max(...months);
  c.move(0, height - (months[0] / max) * height);
  months
    .slice(1)
    .forEach((v, i) =>
      c.line(((i + 1) / (months.length - 1)) * width, height - (v / max) * height),
    );
  c.stroke("#1450aa", { width: 1.5, cap: "round" });
}
</script>

<template>
  <Canvas :height="46" :paint="sparkline" />
</template>
```

The same function works at any width, so one definition serves a wide card and a narrow sidebar.

## Table

`<Table :columns>` holds `<TableRow>`s of `<TableCell>`s. Mark a row `header` to repeat it on every page
the table paginates onto. Columns are widths: a number is fixed points, a string like `"1fr"` is a
flexible share.

```vue
<template>
  <Table :columns="['1fr', 120]" cell-border="#e2e8f0" :cell-padding="9">
    <TableRow header>
      <TableCell><Text bold>Description</Text></TableCell>
      <TableCell><Text bold>Amount</Text></TableCell>
    </TableRow>
    <TableRow v-for="line in lines" :key="line.id">
      <TableCell
        ><Text>{{ line.name }}</Text></TableCell
      >
      <TableCell
        ><Text>{{ line.total }} EUR</Text></TableCell
      >
    </TableRow>
  </Table>
</template>
```

`Table` also takes `gap` / `rowGap` / `colGap`, `cellPadding`, `cellBorder` and a `rule` color.

## Positioned

Out-of-flow placement, anchored to the nearest `<Box relative>` (or the page). Give it edges
(`top` / `right` / `bottom` / `left`) or an alignment (`h` / `v`) plus an `x` / `y` offset.
`:z-index` (since beta.5) sets the paint order - see [Positioning](/docs/pdf/positioning).

```vue
<template>
  <Box relative :height="200">
    <Positioned :top="8" :right="8">
      <Text :size="9" color="#94a3b8">draft</Text>
    </Positioned>
  </Box>
</template>
```

## Navigation

`<Link>` makes its child clickable. `href` opens a URL, `to` jumps to an `<Anchor>` in the same
document. Exactly one of the two.

```vue
<template>
  <Link href="https://jasy.dev">
    <Box bg="#f3dc29" :padding="12"><Text>The whole box is the hit area</Text></Box>
  </Link>
</template>
```

`<Anchor name>` marks a jump target, and `<Bookmark title>` adds an entry to the outline tree your
viewer shows in its sidebar. `level` nests it under the nearest preceding smaller level.

| Component    | Props                       |
| ------------ | --------------------------- |
| `<Link>`     | `href` \| `to`              |
| `<Anchor>`   | `name` (required)           |
| `<Bookmark>` | `title` (required), `level` |

A chapter heading usually wants both: a sidebar entry **and** a jump target. Nest them.

```vue
<template>
  <Bookmark title="2. Installation" :level="1">
    <Anchor name="install">
      <Text :size="22" bold>2. Installation</Text>
    </Anchor>
  </Bookmark>
</template>
```

See [Navigation](/docs/pdf/navigation) for how links, anchors and bookmarks work under the hood.

## Rotated and RotatedBox

`<Rotated :angle>` spins its child at any angle around its center, at paint time: the layout box stays
unrotated, so siblings do not reflow. That is what you want for a stamp or a watermark.

`<RotatedBox :turns>` does layout-aware quarter-turns instead. A 90 or 270 degree turn swaps width and
height, so a vertical label reserves exactly the strip it occupies and its neighbors flow around it.
`turns` counts clockwise 90-degree steps.

```vue
<template>
  <Row :gap="12">
    <RotatedBox :turns="3"><Text bold>SECTION A</Text></RotatedBox>
    <Column><Text>Line one</Text><Text>Line two</Text></Column>
  </Row>

  <Rotated :angle="-18">
    <Box bg="#ffe9e9" border="#d33" :padding="10"
      ><Text :size="26" bold color="#d33">PAID</Text></Box
    >
  </Rotated>
</template>
```

## Page breaks

`<PageBreak />` cuts the flow: everything after it starts on a fresh page. `<KeepTogether>` does the
opposite - it refuses to let its children be split, and moves the whole group to the next page if it
would not fit on this one. Both also exist as props (`break-before`, `break-after`, `keep-together`)
on `<Box>`, `<Column>` and `<Row>`, which is usually the tidier form.

```vue
<template>
  <Page>
    <Text :size="18" bold>Terms</Text>
    <Text>...</Text>

    <PageBreak />

    <Text :size="18" bold>Appendix</Text>

    <KeepTogether>
      <Box border="#d0d4da" :radius="8" :padding="14">
        <Text bold>Signed</Text>
        <Text :size="9" color="gray">This box is never torn across two pages.</Text>
      </Box>
    </KeepTogether>
  </Page>
</template>
```

A break that cannot do anything - inside a `<Row>`, or anywhere that does not paginate - is ignored
rather than obeyed halfway, and says so once on the console. A group taller than a whole page is split
after all, because the alternative is a document that never terminates.

## Columns (since beta.5)

`<SplitView>` sets its content in newspaper columns that continue on the next page and balance on the
last one. `<ColumnBreak />` starts the next column.

```vue
<template>
  <Page :gap="12">
    <Text :size="28" bold color="#1450aa">The Valley Courier</Text>
    <SplitView :columns="3" :colGap="16" :rowGap="8">
      <Text v-for="p in paragraphs" :key="p.id">{{ p.text }}</Text>
    </SplitView>
    <Text italic>This line follows the columns, right where they end.</Text>
  </Page>
</template>
```

For a layout of your own, `<Flow>` takes it as the `#page` slot: one page of the layout, with a
`<Region />` wherever the content goes. The slot gets `{ index, pageNumber }`, so the first page can
look different from the rest.

```vue
<template>
  <Page>
    <Flow :gap="8">
      <template #page="{ index }">
        <Column :gap="12">
          <Text v-if="index === 0" :size="22" bold color="#1450aa">Annual Report</Text>
          <Text v-else :size="9" italic color="gray">Annual Report, continued</Text>
          <Row :gap="16">
            <Expanded><Region /></Expanded>
            <Box bg="#f3f5f9" :padding="8"><Region :width="150" /></Box>
          </Row>
        </Column>
      </template>

      <Text v-for="p in report" :key="p.id">{{ p.text }}</Text>
      <ColumnBreak />
      <Text bold>Notes</Text>
      <Text v-for="n in notes" :key="n.id" :size="8">{{ n.text }}</Text>
    </Flow>
  </Page>
</template>
```

The `#page` slot is rendered for every page while the PDF is laid out, and sees what the components
around it `provide`. Render a document with a `<Flow>` through `renderToPdf`. The options, and the
errors that name a mistake, are on the [Columns](/docs/pdf/columns) page.

## Form fields

A form field is a layout element like any other: it reserves a box, flows with its neighbors, and
emits a widget the reader can actually type into. Seven kinds:

| Component        | For                                                              |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `TextField`      | one line or, with `multiline`, several; `password`, `max-length` |
| `Checkbox`       | a single tick; `on-value` is what gets stored                    |
| `RadioGroup`     | one of several, laid out for you; `options` + `value`            |
| `Dropdown`       | a closed list, or `editable` to allow free text                  |
| `ListBox`        | a visible list; `multi-select` for several at once               |
| `PushButton`     | an action - `"reset"`, `{ open: url }` or `{ submit: url }`      |
| `SignatureField` | an empty signature box for the reader to sign                    |

Every field takes `name` (the key the value is stored under), `required`, `hidden`, `print` and the
appearance props `border`, `background` and `color`. The single widgets add `tooltip`, `read-only` and
`border-width`; the boxed ones (`TextField`, `Dropdown`, `ListBox`, `PushButton`, `SignatureField`) take
`width` and `height`, a `Checkbox` takes `size`. A `RadioGroup` is several buttons, so it has none of
those three: it takes `size`, `gap` and the label styling of its choices.

```vue
<template>
  <Column :gap="10">
    <TextField name="fullName" :width="220" :height="22" border="#aab3c2" background="#fbfcfe" />

    <RadioGroup
      name="plan"
      :gap="6"
      :options="[
        { value: 'basic', label: 'Basic' },
        { value: 'pro', label: 'Pro' },
      ]"
    />

    <Dropdown name="country" :width="110" :height="22" :options="['DE', 'AT', 'CH']" />

    <Checkbox name="agree" label="I have read the statutes" />

    <PushButton name="clear" label="Reset form" action="reset" :width="92" :height="26" />
  </Column>
</template>
```

Give a field a `border` if you want one - a text field draws nothing by default, exactly as a browser
input with `border: none` would.

Reading a form back and filling it is the other half, and lives in the core:
[Forms](/docs/pdf/forms).

## Page numbers

`<PageNumber>` and `<PageCount>` print the current page and the document total. Put them anywhere - a
`#footer` is the usual home, but the body works too. They take the `<Text>` styling props plus `offset`,
which is added to the number (use `-1` when a cover page should not count).

```vue
<template>
  <Document>
    <Page>
      <template #footer>
        <Row justify="center" :gap="3">
          <Text :size="9">Page</Text>
          <PageNumber :size="9" bold />
          <Text :size="9">of</Text>
          <PageCount :size="9" bold />
        </Row>
      </template>
      <Column><!-- body --></Column>
    </Page>
  </Document>
</template>
```

Getting the total right is why jasy paginates the whole document before it draws anything.

`<SubPageNumber>` and `<SubPageCount>` (since beta.2) count within one `<Page>`, for a document
made of sections.

For anything else that depends on the page, `<PageBuilder>` (since beta.2) takes it as its default
scoped slot and builds it for every page it lands on. A slot that renders nothing shows nothing on that
page:

```vue
<template>
  <Page>
    <template #header>
      <PageBuilder #default="{ pageNumber }">
        <Text v-if="pageNumber > 1" :size="9">Annual Report, continued</Text>
      </PageBuilder>
    </template>
    <template #footer>
      <PageBuilder #default="{ pageNumber, pageCount }">
        <Text :size="9" align="center">Page {{ pageNumber }} of {{ pageCount }}</Text>
      </PageBuilder>
    </template>
    <!-- body -->
  </Page>
</template>
```

The slot receives `pageNumber`, `pageCount`, `pageSize`, `subPageNumber` and `subPageTotalPages`, and it
sees what the components around it `provide`. What it builds is placed whole on its page.

## A component of your own

The set above is not closed. `registerElement(type, factory)` teaches the renderer a new node type,
and from then on it is a component like any other - in a Vue template, in a Nuxt page, or in a plain
descriptor tree:

```ts
import { registerElement, Box, Text } from "@jasy/pdf";

registerElement("callout", (props, children) =>
  Box({ bg: "#eef1f5", border: "#1450aa", radius: 6, padding: 12 }, [
    Text(String(children[0] ?? ""), { color: "#1450aa" }),
  ]),
);
```

The seam underneath is `buildDocument(descriptor)`: a `{ type, props, children }` tree resolved
through the same factories the components use. That is exactly how `@jasy/vue` is built - its host
nodes ARE those descriptors - which is why a custom type works in every binding at once, and why a
browser can hand a Node service a document as plain JSON.

react-pdf's primitive set is closed; this one is not.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/vue/data-and-assets
Summary: Drive the page with reactive data, and load custom fonts and images as bytes - in the browser or on a server.

# Data & assets

## Reactive data

The whole point of authoring in Vue is that your data drives the document. `v-for`, `v-if`, `computed`
and slots all work - the renderer walks the same tree Vue builds, so anything that produces a tree
produces a PDF.

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed } from "vue";
import { Document, Page, Row, Text, Divider } from "@jasy/vue";

const props = defineProps<{ lines: { id: number; name: string; price: number }[] }>();
const total = computed(() => props.lines.reduce((sum, l) => sum + l.price, 0));
</script>

<template>
  <Document :size="11">
    <Page :size="'A4'" :margin="48" :gap="8">
      <Row v-for="line in lines" :key="line.id" :justify="'between'">
        <Text>{{ line.name }}</Text>
        <Text>{{ line.price }} EUR</Text>
      </Row>

      <Divider />
      <Row :justify="'between'">
        <Text bold>Total</Text>
        <Text bold>{{ total }} EUR</Text>
      </Row>
    </Page>
  </Document>
</template>
```

A PDF is rendered once, not kept alive like a page: load what the document needs **before**
`renderToPdf` and pass it in as props. A change in `onMounted` (or an async fetch there) comes too late -
the document has been read by then.

## Custom fonts

The standard PDF fonts (Helvetica, Times, Courier) need nothing. To use your own, register the font on
`<Document :fonts>` under a name, then use that name as a `font`. In the browser, fetch the bytes first
and pass them in:

```vue
<!-- Report.vue -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { Document, Page, Text } from "@jasy/vue";

defineProps<{ font: Uint8Array }>();
</script>

<template>
  <Document :fonts="{ Inter: font }" font="Inter">
    <Page size="A4" :margin="48">
      <Text :size="24" bold>Set in Inter</Text>
    </Page>
  </Document>
</template>
```

```ts
const font = new Uint8Array(await (await fetch("/fonts/Inter.woff2")).arrayBuffer());
const bytes = await renderToPdf(Report, { font });
```

The container does not matter: **`.ttf`, `.woff` and `.woff2` are the same thing here** - jasy unwraps
the wrapper itself. Full Unicode comes with it, and the font is subsetted on the way into the PDF, so
the file stays small. For weights, register one file per style as
`{ Inter: { normal, bold, italic } }`.

On the **server** (Nuxt's `definePdfHandler`, or any Node process) a plain path works too - there
`:fonts="{ Inter: '/path/to/Inter.woff2' }"` is the whole story. In the browser there is no filesystem
to point at, so it is bytes.

## Images

`<Image :src>` takes the image bytes as a `Uint8Array`, a URL, or - on a server - a path. JPEG and PNG
both work, and PNG transparency is honored: it composites over whatever sits behind it, not a white box.
Bytes arrive the same way as a font, as a prop:

```vue
<template>
  <Image :src="logo" :width="120" :height="40" fit="contain" />
</template>
```

A URL is fetched while the document is prepared, before the layout runs, so its size is known when the
page is laid out.

## Render options

`renderToPdf` (and `renderToPdfString`) take the engine's render options as their third argument:

```ts
const bytes = await renderToPdf(Invoice, props, {
  onOverflow: "warn",
  accessible: true,
  encrypt: { userPassword: "secret" },
  onDiagnostic: (d) => console.log(d.code, d.message),
});
```

- `onOverflow` - what happens when a single unbreakable element is taller than the page: `"error"`
  (default) throws, `"warn"` places it clipped and logs, `"ignore"` places it clipped.
- `accessible` - a tagged PDF with a structure tree for screen readers, see
  [Accessibility](/docs/pdf/accessibility).
- `encrypt` - AES-256 password protection, see [Encryption](/docs/pdf/encryption).
- `onDiagnostic` - everything the engine has to say about the document, one call per finding, see
  [Output](/docs/pdf/output).

## A descriptor for a server

`toDocumentDescriptor(Component, props)` stops before the PDF and returns the engine's descriptor: a plain
`{ type, props, children }` tree that `buildDocument` turns into the document. To post it as JSON, encode
font and image bytes yourself - JSON has no `Uint8Array` - and decode them on the other side. Functions do
not survive JSON at all, so a document with a `<Canvas>`, a `<Flow>` or a `<PageBuilder>` goes through
`renderToPdf`.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/nuxt
Summary: The @jasy/nuxt module - author PDFs as Vue components and render them in the browser or on a server route, zero config.

# PDFs in Nuxt

`@jasy/nuxt` is the Nuxt module for [`@jasy/vue`](/docs/vue) and [`@jasy/pdf`](/docs/pdf). Add it to
`modules` and the components and render helpers are just there - no imports, no wiring. Render a PDF in
the browser with `usePdf`, or stream one from a Nitro route with `definePdfHandler`.

## Install

```bash
npx nuxi module add @jasy/nuxt
```

That installs the package and registers it for you. Or do it by hand:

```bash
pnpm add @jasy/nuxt
```

```ts
// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  modules: ["@jasy/nuxt"],
});
```

## Client: `usePdf`

Author a PDF as a Vue component. The jasy components are auto-registered, so there is nothing to import:

```vue
<!-- Invoice.vue -->
<template>
  <Document :size="11">
    <Page :size="'A4'" :margin="48">
      <Text :size="24" bold color="#0a2348">Invoice #{{ id }}</Text>
    </Page>
  </Document>
</template>
```

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import Invoice from "./Invoice.vue";

const { open, download, pending } = usePdf(Invoice, { props: { id: 42 } });
</script>

<template>
  <button :disabled="pending" @click="open">View PDF</button>
</template>
```

`open()` and `download()` render on demand and reuse the result, so one click is one render. Pass
`{ immediate: true }` to pre-render on mount.

## Server: `definePdfHandler`

The `@jasy/pdf` tree API is auto-imported in `server/`. No Vue, no browser - build the document and stream
it:

```ts
// server/api/invoice/[id].get.ts
export default definePdfHandler((event) =>
  Document([
    Page({ size: "A4", margin: 48 }, [
      Text(`Invoice #${getRouterParam(event, "id")}`, { size: 24, bold: true }),
    ]),
  ]),
);
```

`GET /api/invoice/42` streams `application/pdf`. Need auth or a data fetch first? Use
`sendPdf(event, doc, opts)` inside your own handler, or `renderToBytes(doc)` to just get the bytes - save
them, attach them to an email, anything.

### Caching

Wrap a route in Nitro's cache. The key is the request path + query, so it caches per request out of the
box:

```ts
export default definePdfHandler(build, { cache: { maxAge: 3600 } });
```

Expired entries re-render fresh (`swr` is off by default), so a stale invoice is never served.

## Options

```ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  modules: ["@jasy/nuxt"],
  jasy: {
    autoImport: true, // auto-register components + the tree API (default true)
    prefix: "Pdf", // <PdfDocument> in templates, PdfDocument(...) in server/ (default none)
  },
});
```

### Use a prefix

The default is none, and that is the risky setting: unprefixed auto-imports really are named `Text`,
`Row`, `Box` and `Image` - and Nuxt UI, most component libraries and even the DOM already claim some of
those. Setting `prefix: "Jasy"` or `"Pdf"` costs you five characters per tag and removes a whole class
of confusing collisions. It applies to both sides, so the server factories match the components.

## Where to next

- [**PDFs in Vue**](/docs/vue) - the components and `renderToPdf`, in depth. Everything there is
  available here too, `<Svg>` and `<Canvas>` included - the module only registers the same components
  under your prefix.
- [**Creating PDFs**](/docs/pdf) - the underlying engine and its tree API.

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/react
Summary: Author PDFs as React components with @jasy/react and render them right in the browser - or on a server, the same call.

# PDFs in React (since beta.1)

`@jasy/react` lets you author a PDF the way you build an app: a tree of components, with props, hooks,
context and your own data. It is a thin React renderer over the [`@jasy/pdf`](/docs/pdf) engine, so you
get its real layout and pagination - and because the engine is isomorphic, `renderToPdf` produces the
PDF bytes **right in the browser**. No headless browser, no server round-trip, no Java.

A document in JSX renders byte for byte like the same document written with the `@jasy/pdf` functions,
and every prop is typed by the engine's own option types.

## Install

```bash
pnpm add @jasy/react @jasy/pdf react
```

React 19 (every 19.x). `@jasy/pdf` and `react` are peer dependencies, so your app has exactly one copy
of each.

## Your first PDF component

A document's root is always `<Document>`. Everything else nests inside, exactly like the engine's
element tree. Text is children, as anywhere in React.

```tsx
// Invoice.tsx
import { Box, Divider, Document, Page, Row, Text } from "@jasy/react";

export function Invoice({ customer, total }: { customer: string; total: number }) {
  return (
    <Document size={11} color="#1f2937">
      <Page size="A4" margin={48} gap={16}>
        <Text size={24} bold color="#0a2348">
          Invoice #2026-001
        </Text>
        <Text color="#64748b">Billed to: {customer}</Text>
        <Divider color="#e2e8f0" />

        <Row justify="between">
          <Text>Consulting</Text>
          <Text bold>{total} EUR</Text>
        </Row>

        <Box bg="#0a2348" padding={12} radius={6}>
          <Text color="#f3dc29" bold>
            Total due: {total} EUR
          </Text>
        </Box>
      </Page>
    </Document>
  );
}
```

## Render it to a PDF

`renderToPdf` takes an element and returns the PDF as a `Uint8Array`. In the browser:

```tsx
import { renderToPdf } from "@jasy/react";
import { Invoice } from "./Invoice";

export function DownloadButton() {
  async function download() {
    const bytes = await renderToPdf(<Invoice customer="ACME GmbH" total={1190} />);
    const url = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([bytes], { type: "application/pdf" }));
    window.open(url);
  }
  return <button onClick={download}>Download invoice</button>;
}
```

On a server it is the same call - write the bytes to a file or send them as a response:

```tsx
import { writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { renderToPdf } from "@jasy/react";
import { Invoice } from "./Invoice";

await writeFile("invoice.pdf", await renderToPdf(<Invoice customer="ACME GmbH" total={1190} />));
```

Need the raw PDF string instead of bytes? Use `renderToPdfString`. A component that throws fails the
render with that error, so a broken document never comes out half-drawn.

## Where to next

- [**Components**](/docs/react/components) - the full set, their props, header and footer, page numbers.
- [**Data & assets**](/docs/react/data-and-assets) - your data, custom fonts and images, render options.
- [**Creating PDFs**](/docs/pdf) - the underlying engine, its layout primitives and pagination.

To see it all running, clone the repo and start the playground: twelve documents rendered in your
browser, side by side with their source.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/jasy-pdf/jasy && cd jasy && pnpm install && pnpm run build
pnpm --filter @jasy/react play
```

---

Source: https://jasy.dev/docs/react/components
Summary: The @jasy/react component set, their typed props, header and footer, page numbers and flowing layouts.

# Components

Every component maps to one engine element, and every prop type IS the engine's option type: a new
engine option is a typed prop the day it ships, and a wrong value goes red in your editor. Boolean props
have the usual JSX shorthand: `<Text bold>` is `<Text bold={true}>`.

The full set:

`Document` · `Page` · `Column` · `Row` · `Box` · `Padding` · `Expanded` · `Spacer` · `Divider` ·
`Image` · `Svg` · `Canvas` · `Text` · `Paragraph` · `Span` · `Table` / `TableRow` / `TableCell` ·
`Positioned` · `DefaultTextStyle` · `Link` · `Anchor` · `Bookmark` · `Rotated` · `RotatedBox` ·
`PageBreak` · `KeepTogether` · `PageNumber` · `PageCount` · `SubPageNumber` · `SubPageCount` ·
`PageBuilder` · `SplitView` · `Flow` · `Region` · `ColumnBreak` · `TextField` · `Checkbox` ·
`RadioGroup` · `Dropdown` · `ListBox` · `PushButton` · `SignatureField`.

Where React has its own way, it is used: text and labels are children, repeating areas are props, and
what is built per page is a function.

## Structure

### Document

The root of every PDF. Its text props set the document-wide defaults that everything inside inherits.

| Prop                                      | Type                                                           |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `size`, `color`, `font`, `bold`, `italic` | default text style - any inheritable text style                |
